title: श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता — साङ्ख्ययोगः
titleEn: The Bhagavad Gītā — Chapter 2: The Yoga of Knowledge
draftNote: Prepared by the Lectorium pipeline from the vulgate text, with a drafting pass, a reviewing pass and a mechanical gate; a printed-edition collation and audio are still to come. Use ⚑ correction on any verse to report a problem.
source: Text: the received (vulgate) text of the Bhagavadgītā, Mahābhārata 6.23–40, as read by Śaṅkara's commentary. Devanagari from Sanskrit Wikisource (भगवद्गीता/साङ्ख्ययोगः), collated verse by verse against the GRETIL romanized text based on the BORI critical edition (input Tokunaga, rev. J. Smith); every verse where the two differ carries a note giving the BORI reading, and every correction to the Wikisource text is named in its note. Collation against a pre-1930 printed edition is still to be done. Transliteration: IAST. The reading under each word gives the words with sandhi undone and compound members hyphenated, in the manner of the traditional pada-pāṭha. Pronunciation convention: classical Sanskrit as described in Whitney's Sanskrit Grammar (1889); no audio yet. Translations made fresh from the Sanskrit with Monier-Williams (1899), Apte (1890) and Śaṅkara's commentary for the traditional sense; no modern translation consulted.

sentences.t: सञ्जय उवाच
sentences.tr: sañjaya uvāca
sentences.l: Sañjaya said

morph.gloss: Sañjaya, the king's minister and charioteer, who reports the battle to him (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
तं तथा कृपयाविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम् ।
विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः ॥
sentences.tr:
tam tathā kṛpayā āviṣṭam aśru-pūrṇa-ākula-īkṣaṇam |
viṣīdantam idam vākyam uvāca madhusūdanaḥ ||

morph.gloss: that, he (tam: acc. sg. masc., anticipating Arjuna)
to enter, come over (āviṣṭam: past participle 'overcome', acc. sg. masc.; kṛpayā + ā- → kṛpayā- with the like vowels merging)
eye (aśru-pūrṇa-ākula-īkṣaṇa: bahuvrīhi 'whose eyes are full of tears and troubled', acc. sg. masc.)
to sink, despair (viṣīdantam: present participle, acc. sg. masc. 'despairing')
this (idam: acc. sg. neut., anticipating vākyam)
'slayer of the demon Madhu', Kṛṣṇa (nom. sg.)

sentences.l: Him thus, by-pity-overcome, whose-eyes-were-tear-filled-and-troubled, despairing — this word Madhusūdana spoke.
sentences.i: To him — overcome with pity like this, his eyes filled with tears and troubled, sunk in despair — Madhusūdana spoke these words.
sentences.n: The chapter opens mid-scene: Kṛṣṇa, called here Madhusūdana ('slayer of Madhu'), answers Arjuna, whose collapse closed chapter 1. Kṛpayāviṣṭam is kṛpayā + āviṣṭam, 'entered by pity' — the same āviṣṭa- construction used of Arjuna's grief in 1.28 (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ); the grief named there is the target of Kṛṣṇa's first words here. Aśru-pūrṇa-ākula-īkṣaṇam is a bahuvrīhi (possessive compound): 'having eyes that are tear-filled and troubled'.

sentences.t: श्रीभगवानुवाच
sentences.tr: śrībhagavān uvāca
sentences.l: The Blessed Lord said

morph.gloss: the Blessed One, the Lord — Kṛṣṇa's title as speaker (nom. sg. bhagavān; -n + u- written joined)

sentences.t:
कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम् ।
अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन ॥
sentences.tr:
kutaḥ tvā kaśmalam idam viṣame samupasthitam |
anārya-juṣṭam asvargyam akīrti-karam arjuna ||

morph.gloss: whence, from where (interrog. adverb; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
dirt, taint; despondency, weakness (acc. sg. neut.)
uneven, difficult, critical (loc. sg. 'at this critical moment')
to come upon, present itself (samupasthitam: past participle, acc. sg. neut. 'has come upon [you]')
ignoble, unworthy of an Ārya (first compound member)
resorted to, practiced (an-ārya-juṣṭa: 'practiced by the ignoble', acc. sg. neut.)
not leading to heaven (acc. sg. neut.)
making, causing (akīrti-kara: 'bringing disgrace', acc. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: Whence to-you this confusion, at-a-critical-moment come-upon — practiced-by-the-ignoble, not-leading-to-heaven, disgrace-causing, Arjuna?
sentences.i: Where has this weakness of yours come from at this critical moment, Arjuna? It is unworthy of a noble man, it leads to no heaven, and it brings only disgrace.
sentences.n: Kaśmala, 'taint, despondency', is a strong word — Kṛṣṇa treats Arjuna's collapse as a moral failure, not mere sensitivity. Three adjectives follow in a row, all built the same way: anārya-juṣṭam 'practiced by the ignoble' (an-ārya, someone without the values of a well-bred Ārya), asvargyam 'not leading to svarga (heaven)', akīrti-karam 'disgrace-making'. This is the first verse of Kṛṣṇa's teaching, which runs with only brief interruptions to the end of the poem.

sentences.t:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते ।
क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप ॥
sentences.tr:
klaibyam mā sma gamaḥ pārtha na etat tvayi upapadyate |
kṣudram hṛdaya-daurbalyam tyaktvā uttiṣṭha parantapa ||

morph.gloss: particle strengthening a prohibition with mā ('never')
to go (gamaḥ: aorist injunctive 2nd sg., with mā: 'do not go to, do not yield to')
this (etat: nom. sg. neut., referring to klaibyam; na + e- → nai-)
to be fitting, befit (upapadyate: present middle 3rd sg. 'is fitting'; -i + u- → -y u-)
weakness, feebleness (hṛdaya-daurbalya: 'weakness of heart', acc. sg. neut.)
to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund 'having cast off'; -ā + u- → -o-)
to stand up, arise (uttiṣṭha: imperative 2nd sg. 'arise!')
'scorcher of the enemy', a warrior's epithet (vocative, addressed here to Arjuna)

sentences.l: Unmanliness do not go-to, Pārtha; this in-you does not befit. Petty heart-weakness having-cast-off, arise, O scorcher-of-the-foe.
sentences.i: Do not give way to unmanliness, Pārtha — it does not become you. Cast off this petty faintheartedness and rise up, scorcher of the foe.
sentences.n: Mā gamaḥ, 'do not go [to]', is the aorist injunctive used with mā in prohibitions rather than the ordinary imperative — a construction that will recur through the poem. Klaibya, 'the state of a klība (an impotent man)', is a pointed insult to a warrior. Hṛdaya-daurbalyam, 'weakness of heart', is Kṛṣṇa's diagnosis of what chapter 1 showed; parantapa, 'scorcher of the foe', is an epithet elsewhere used of Arjuna himself.

sentences.t: अर्जुन उवाच
sentences.tr: arjuna uvāca
sentences.l: Arjuna said

morph.gloss: Arjuna, the third Pāṇḍava, the great archer (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन ।
इषुभिः प्रति योत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन ॥
sentences.tr:
katham bhīṣmam aham saṃkhye droṇam ca madhusūdana |
iṣubhiḥ prati yotsyāmi pūjā-arhau ari-sūdana ||

morph.gloss: Droṇa, teacher of both sides (acc. sg.)
to fight (yotsyāmi: future 1st sg. 'I shall fight')
worthy, deserving (pūjā-arha: 'worthy of honor', acc. dual, of Bhīṣma and Droṇa together; -au + a- → -āv a-)
slayer, destroyer (ari-sūdana: 'slayer of enemies', vocative, to Kṛṣṇa)

sentences.l: How Bhīṣma I in-battle, and Droṇa, with-arrows against shall-I-fight, O slayer-of-Madhu — the-two-worthy-of-honor, O slayer-of-foes?
sentences.i: How can I meet Bhīṣma and Droṇa with arrows in battle, Madhusūdana? Both of them deserve my worship, slayer of enemies.
sentences.n: Arjuna answers with a question, not yet an argument — a rhetorical 'how?' (katham) that frames the whole speech running to verse 37. Pūjārhau, 'the two worthy of worship, of honor' (one dual adjective covering Bhīṣma and Droṇa together), states his real objection: these are not enemies to him but venerated elders. Ari-sūdana, 'slayer of foes', is one more epithet of Kṛṣṇa alongside Madhusūdana in the same verse — names of the god pile up even as Arjuna refuses violence.

sentences.t:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान् श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके ।
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान् ॥
sentences.tr:
gurūn ahatvā hi mahā-anubhāvān śreyaḥ bhoktum bhaikṣyam api iha loke |
hatvā artha-kāmān tu gurūn iha eva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhira-pradigdhān ||

morph.gloss: to not kill (ahatvā: negative gerund 'without killing')
majesty, dignity, greatness (mahā-anubhāva: 'of great majesty', acc. pl.; -ā + a- → -ā-)
the better thing, the good (nom. sg. neut.; -aḥ before bh- → -o)
alms, beggar's food (acc. sg. neut.; see note on the BORI reading)
desiring (artha-kāma: 'desiring gain', acc. pl. bahuvrīhi describing the teachers; -n + t- → -ṃs t-)
here, in this world (iha + eva → ihaiva)
to enjoy (bhuñjīya: optative middle 1st sg. 'I would enjoy')
to smear (pradigdha: past participle 'smeared'; rudhira-pradigdha: 'blood-smeared', acc. pl.)

sentences.l: The-teachers not-having-killed, indeed, of-great-majesty — better it-is to-eat even alms-food here in-the-world; but the-teachers-desiring-gain having-killed, here indeed I-would-enjoy enjoyments blood-smeared.
sentences.i: Better to live here in this world on beggar's food, without killing these teachers of such greatness, than to enjoy, after killing them, pleasures smeared with the blood of teachers grown greedy for gain.
sentences.n: Gurūn, 'the teachers', covers both Bhīṣma and Droṇa; Arjuna argues that killing an elder poisons every pleasure that could follow, however compromised the elders' own motives (artha-kāmān, 'desiring wealth', hints that Bhīṣma and Droṇa fight for Duryodhana's cause, not conviction). Bhaikṣya, 'living on alms', is the diet of a renunciant who has given up the world — a striking alternative for a kṣatriya to name. The vulgate reads bhaikṣyam here; the BORI critical edition reads bhaikṣam instead, the same word without the -ya- suffix and with no difference of sense.

sentences.t:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः ।
यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम- स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥
sentences.tr:
na ca etat vidmaḥ katarat naḥ garīyaḥ yad vā jayema yadi vā naḥ jayeyuḥ |
yān eva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaḥ te avasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ ||

morph.gloss: this (etat: acc. sg. neut., the choice about to be named)
which of two (katarat: nom. sg. neut. interrogative; -t + n- → -n n-)
weightier, more important (comparative of guru; nom. sg. neut.; -aḥ before y- → -o)
to conquer (jayema: optative 1st pl. 'we might conquer')
I (naḥ: enclitic acc. pl. 'us'; -aḥ before j- → -o)
to conquer (jayeyuḥ: optative 3rd pl. 'they might conquer')
who, which (yān: acc. pl. masc. relative, 'those whom')
to live (jijīviṣāmaḥ: desiderative present 1st pl. 'we should wish to live'; the Wikisource line breaks this word oddly across the print line — see note)
that, they (te: nom. pl. masc., the Kauravas; -aḥ + t- → -as t-, completing jijīviṣāmaḥ from the previous token)
to stand, be arrayed (avasthitāḥ: past participle, nom. pl.; te + a- → te 'vasthitāḥ)
foremost, facing, in front (loc. sg. 'facing, in the front rank')
son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the Kaurava host collectively (nom. pl.)

sentences.l: And this we-do-not-know, which for-us [would-be] the-weightier — whether we-should-conquer, or if they-should-conquer us — those very ones, having-killed whom we-should-not-wish-to-live, stand-arrayed facing [us]: the-sons-of-Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
sentences.i: We do not even know which would be better for us — that we should conquer, or that we should be conquered. If we killed them, the very men now arrayed before us, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, we would not wish to go on living.
sentences.n: Yān eva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaḥ, 'those very men, having killed whom we should not wish to live' — Arjuna names his real fear for the first time: not death, but surviving the killing. The Wikisource text breaks the phrase jijīviṣāmas te 'vasthitāḥ oddly across a print line, splitting it into जिजीविषाम- and स्तेऽवस्थिताः; the two are one continuous phrase (jijīviṣāmaḥ + te + avasthitāḥ) and are drafted here as two words-entries only to tile the source exactly. Garīyaḥ, 'weightier, more important', is the comparative of guru — the same guru who is 'heavy' gives the ordinary word for 'teacher'.

sentences.t:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेताः ।
यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥
sentences.tr:
kārpaṇya-doṣa-upahata-svabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvām dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetāḥ |
yat śreyaḥ syāt niścitam brūhi tat me śiṣyaḥ te aham śādhi mām tvām prapannam ||

morph.gloss: wretchedness, weakness of spirit (first compound member)
afflicted, struck (past participle of upa-han; -a + u- → -o-)
nature, own-being (kārpaṇya-doṣa-upahata-svabhāva: 'whose nature is afflicted by the fault of weakness', nom. sg. masc.)
mind (dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetas: 'whose mind is confused about dharma', nom. sg. masc.)
which, what (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative; -t + ś- → -c ch-)
the better thing, the good (nom. sg. neut.)
to be (syāt: optative 3rd sg. 'may be'; -t + n- → -n n-)
that (tat: acc. sg. neut., referring to śreyaḥ; -t + m- → -n m-)
you (te: enclitic gen. sg. 'your'; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
I (nom. sg.; te + a- → te 'with avagraha)
to instruct, rule, teach (śādhi: imperative 2nd sg. 'instruct!')
you (tvām: acc. sg., the goal of prapannam)
to approach, take refuge in (prapannam: past participle, acc. sg. masc., agreeing with mām: 'having taken refuge')

sentences.l: By-the-fault-of-weakness-afflicted-in-my-nature, I-ask you, whose-mind-is-confused-about-dharma: which [is] the-better — certain — tell that to-me. Your-pupil I [am]; instruct me, come-to-you-for-refuge.
sentences.i: My very nature is struck down by the weakness of pity, and my mind is confused about dharma; I ask you — tell me for certain what is truly better. I am your pupil: teach me, for I have come to you for refuge.
sentences.n: This is the pivot of the poem: Arjuna finally names what has happened to him (kārpaṇya, 'wretchedness, weakness of spirit', the noun behind klaibya in verse 3) and, unable to see his own dharma, formally asks to be taught. Śiṣyas te 'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam, 'I am your pupil — teach me, who have come to you for refuge', is the moment Arjuna becomes a student rather than a friend giving orders; the rest of the poem answers this request. Prapanna, 'one who has taken refuge', returns at the house rendering of 18.66.

sentences.t:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद् यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् ।
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
sentences.tr:
na hi prapaśyāmi mama apanudyāt yat śokam ucchoṣaṇam indriyāṇām |
avāpya bhūmau asapatnam ṛddham rājyam surāṇām api ca adhipatyam ||

morph.gloss: to see clearly, discern (prapaśyāmi: present 1st sg. 'I see, discern')
to drive away, dispel (apanudyāt: optative 3rd sg. 'might dispel'; -a + a- → -ā-)
which, that (yat: acc. sg. neut. relative, referring to śokam; -t + ś- → -cch-)
to dry up, wither (ucchoṣaṇa: 'withering, desiccating', acc. sg. neut., in apposition to śokam)
earth (bhūmau: loc. sg. 'on earth'; -au + a- → -āv a-)
without a rival, unopposed (acc. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: For I-do-not-see-clearly what might-dispel this grief that-withers the-senses, even having-obtained on-earth an-unrivaled and-flourishing kingdom, or even overlordship of-the-gods.
sentences.i: I cannot see what could dispel this grief that is drying up my senses, even if I won a kingdom on earth, unrivaled and prosperous, or lordship over the gods themselves.
sentences.n: Arjuna's despair is stated here as total: no worldly prize, however great, could touch it — not even sovereignty over the gods (surāṇām ādhipatyam), the largest thing the epic imagination can name. This closes the question that Kṛṣṇa's teaching, beginning at verse 11, will answer — not by offering Arjuna a bigger prize, but by changing what grief and prize mean to him.

sentences.t: सञ्जय उवाच
sentences.tr: sañjaya uvāca
sentences.l: Sañjaya said

morph.gloss: Sañjaya, the king's minister and charioteer, who reports the battle to him (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप ।
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह ॥
sentences.tr:
evam uktvā hṛṣīkeśam guḍākeśaḥ parantapa |
na yotsye iti govindam uktvā tūṣṇīm babhūva ha ||

morph.gloss: 'scorcher of the enemy' (vocative, addressed here to Dhṛtarāṣṭra)
to fight (yotsye: future middle 1st sg. 'I shall fight'; yotsye + iti → yotsya iti, see note)
thus (closes the quoted words 'I will not fight')

sentences.l: Thus having-spoken to-the-Lord-of-the-senses, Guḍākeśa, O scorcher-of-the-foe: 'I will not fight' — thus, having-spoken to-Govinda, silent he-became, indeed.
sentences.i: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa said, O scorcher of the foe: 'I will not fight' — and having said this to Govinda, he fell silent.
sentences.n: The narrator's voice returns, and the whole speech from verse 4 closes on the flat declarative na yotsya iti, 'I will not fight'. Yotsya iti is a stock example of Sanskrit sandhi: the verb yotsye, ending in -e, is realized as yotsya before the quotation-marker iti. Parantapa here addresses Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as throughout the frame; Guḍākeśa and Hṛṣīkeśa are, as before, Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.

sentences.t:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः ॥
sentences.tr:
tam uvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasan iva bhārata |
senayoḥ ubhayoḥ madhye viṣīdantam idam vacaḥ ||

morph.gloss: that, he (tam: acc. sg. masc., referring to Arjuna)
to smile, laugh (prahasan: present participle, nom. sg. 'smiling'; -n + i- → -nn-)
descendant of Bharata (vocative, addressed to Dhṛtarāṣṭra)
to sink, despair (viṣīdantam: present participle, acc. sg. masc., referring to Arjuna)
this (idam: acc. sg. neut., anticipating vacaḥ)

sentences.l: Him said Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling as-it-were, O Bhārata, between the-two-armies, to-the-one-despairing, this word.
sentences.i: To him, Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling as it were, spoke this word between the two armies, Bhārata, to Arjuna sunk in despair.
sentences.n: Prahasann iva, 'smiling, as it were', is the poem's only note of Kṛṣṇa's manner before he begins to teach; Śaṅkara reads the smile as amusement that a wise man's grief should be for the body, when the truth about to be stated is that the self cannot die. Senayor ubhayor madhye, 'between the two armies', repeats 1.21 verbatim, closing the frame opened there.

sentences.t: श्रीभगवानुवाच
sentences.tr: śrībhagavān uvāca
sentences.l: The Blessed Lord said

morph.gloss: the Blessed One, the Lord — Kṛṣṇa's title as speaker (nom. sg. bhagavān; -n + u- written joined)

sentences.t:
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे ।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः ॥
sentences.tr:
aśocyān anvaśocaḥ tvam prajñā-vādān ca bhāṣase |
gata-asūn agata-asūn ca na anuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ ||

morph.gloss: not to be grieved for (gerundive of śuc with negative a-; acc. pl. masc.)
to grieve for, mourn (anvaśocaḥ: imperfect 2nd sg. 'you grieved for'; anu + a- → anv-a-)
talk, speech, argument (prajñā-vāda: 'words of wisdom', acc. pl.; -n + c- → -ṃś c-)
to speak (bhāṣase: present middle 2nd sg. 'you speak')
life-breath, life (gata-asu: 'whose life-breath has departed', i.e. dead; acc. pl.; -a + a- → -ā-)
life-breath (a-gata-asu: 'whose life-breath has not departed', i.e. living; acc. pl.)
to grieve for (anuśocanti: present 3rd pl. 'they grieve')

sentences.l: For-those-not-to-be-grieved-for you-grieved, and words-of-wisdom you-speak; for-those-whose-breath-has-gone and-for-those-whose-breath-has-not-gone the-wise do-not-grieve.
sentences.i: You grieve for those not to be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa's teaching begins with a paradox stated in one line: Arjuna talks like a paṇḍita (a learned man) while acting like a fool, grieving for men who do not deserve grief. Gatāsūn agatāsūn, 'those whose breath has gone' and 'those whose breath has not gone' — the dead and the living — is the first hint of the argument to come: that the distinction between dead and alive is not, at the deepest level, the one that matters. This opens the section on the immortality of the self that runs to verse 30.

sentences.t:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः ।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम् ॥
sentences.tr:
na tu eva aham jātu na āsam na tvam na ime janādhipāḥ |
na ca eva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayam ataḥ param ||

morph.gloss: lord, ruler (jana-adhipa: 'lord of men, king', nom. pl.)
to be (bhaviṣyāmaḥ: future 1st pl. 'we shall be')
further, beyond (param: adverbial acc., with atas: 'hereafter')

sentences.l: For never indeed I did-not-exist, nor you, nor these lords-of-men; nor indeed shall-we-not-be, all of-us, hereafter.
sentences.i: There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor will there ever be a time hereafter when any of us ceases to be.
sentences.n: The first positive claim of the teaching: not merely that the self does not die in this one death, but that it has always existed and always will — na tv evāhaṃ jātu nāsam, 'for indeed I never did not exist'. Kṛṣṇa speaks of himself, Arjuna, and 'these kings' (janādhipāḥ, the assembled warriors) all in the same breath, as if from outside time looking at the whole scene at once — a first glimpse of the more explicit divine claim that comes only in chapter 4 and after.

sentences.t:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा ।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
sentences.tr:
dehinaḥ asmin yathā dehe kaumāram yauvanam jarā |
tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ dhīraḥ tatra na muhyati ||

morph.gloss: the embodied one, the possessor of a body (dehinaḥ: gen. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
this (asmin: loc. sg. masc., agreeing with dehe)
attainment, obtaining (deha-antara-prāpti: 'the obtaining of another body', nom. sg.; -iḥ + dh- → -ir dh-)
steady, wise, resolute (nom. sg.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
there, in that (i.e. in the face of this)
to be confused, deluded (muhyati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Of-the-embodied-one, in-this body, as [there is] childhood, youth, old-age, so [there is] the-attaining-of-another-body; the-steady-one there does-not-become-confused.
sentences.i: Just as the embodied self passes, in this body, through childhood, youth and old age, so too it passes into another body; the wise man is not confused by this.
sentences.n: The argument's central image: the self (dehin, 'the embodied one', the ātman as it possesses a body) already changes bodies constantly within one lifetime — child to youth to old man — so passing into a wholly different body at death (dehāntara-prāpti) is nothing new in kind, only in degree. Dhīra, 'steady, resolute', becomes one of the poem's recurring words for the man who is not shaken (compare verse 15, and muni at verse 56). This is the first statement of what later tradition calls reincarnation, argued here purely by analogy with the body's own changes.

sentences.t:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः ।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥
sentences.tr:
mātrā-sparśāḥ tu kaunteya śīta-uṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ |
āgama-apāyinaḥ anityāḥ tān titikṣasva bhārata ||

morph.gloss: matter, an element, a measure (first compound member; here: sense-objects)
giving (śīta-uṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-da: 'giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain', nom. pl.)
going away, departing (āgama-apāyin: 'coming and going', nom. pl.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
that (tān: acc. pl. masc., referring to mātrāsparśāḥ)
to be sharp, endure (titikṣasva: desiderative-formation imperative middle 2nd sg. 'endure! bear patiently!')
descendant of Bharata (vocative, addressed here to Arjuna)

sentences.l: The-sense-contacts, indeed, O son-of-Kuntī, giving-cold-and-heat-and-pleasure-and-pain, coming-and-going, impermanent — them endure, O Bhārata.
sentences.i: The contacts of the senses with their objects, Kaunteya, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go; they are impermanent. Endure them, Bhārata.
sentences.n: Mātrā-sparśāḥ, 'sense-contacts' (mātrā here in the old sense of an element or measure of experience), names what both chapter 1's symptoms of shock and chapter 2's grief are: sensations, arising from contact between sense and object, that come and go like weather. Āgamāpāyinaḥ, 'coming and going', a bahuvrīhi, states their nature directly; titikṣasva, 'endure them', is the practical instruction that follows from that nature, before the metaphysical argument about the self resumes in the next verse.

sentences.t:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ ।
समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते ॥
sentences.tr:
yam hi na vyathayanti ete puruṣam puruṣa-ṛṣabha |
sama-duḥkha-sukham dhīram saḥ amṛtatvāya kalpate ||

morph.gloss: who, whom (yam: acc. sg. masc. relative)
to be disturbed, shaken (vyathayanti: causative present 3rd pl. 'they disturb'; -i + e- → -y e-)
this (ete: nom. pl., referring to mātrāsparśāḥ, 'these')
bull; puruṣa-ṛṣabha 'bull among men', addressed to Arjuna (vocative; -a + ṛ- → -ar-)
pleasure (sama-duḥkha-sukha: 'to whom pain and pleasure are equal', acc. sg. masc.)
that, he (saḥ: nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
to be fit for, be equal to (kalpate: present middle 3rd sg. 'is fit for, becomes able for')

sentences.l: Whom indeed these [sense-contacts] do-not-disturb, [that] man, O bull-among-men, to-whom-pain-and-pleasure-are-equal, steady — he for-immortality becomes-fit.
sentences.i: The man whom these sensations do not disturb, bull among men, who is unmoved alike by pleasure and pain, steady — he is fit for immortality.
sentences.n: Amṛtatva, 'the state of amṛta, deathlessness', names for the first time the goal the whole teaching aims at; kalpate, 'is fit for, is equal to [the task of]', treats immortality as something to be qualified for by a settled character, not simply granted. Sama-duḥkha-sukham, 'to whom pain and pleasure are equal', is a compound that recurs almost verbatim later in the poem and becomes a name for equanimity itself.

sentences.t:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः ।
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥
sentences.tr:
na asataḥ vidyate bhāvaḥ na abhāvaḥ vidyate sataḥ |
ubhayoḥ api dṛṣṭaḥ antaḥ tu anayoḥ tattva-darśibhiḥ ||

morph.gloss: to find, exist (vidyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'there is found, there exists')
being, existence, coming-into-being (nom. sg.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
to find, exist (vidyate: present passive 3rd sg.)
the existent, being, real (sataḥ: gen. sg. neut.)
both (ubhayoḥ: gen. dual, referring to sat and asat)
to see (dṛṣṭa: past participle 'seen', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
end, boundary, conclusion (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
this (anayoḥ: gen. dual, referring to sat and asat)
truth, true nature, reality (first compound member)
seeing, one who sees (tattva-darśin: 'seer of the truth', instr. pl.)

sentences.l: Of-the-non-existent there-is-found no coming-to-be; of-the-existent there-is-found no ceasing-to-be; of-both indeed, seen [is] the-conclusion, of-these-two, by-the-seers-of-truth.
sentences.i: Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no non-being. This conclusion, about both, has been seen by the seers of truth.
sentences.n: The famous line that grounds the whole argument: bhāva and abhāva ('coming to be' and 'not being') simply cannot apply to asat and sat (the unreal and the real) respectively — what is real cannot stop being real, and what is unreal never was real to begin with. The second half names the source of this claim directly: tattva-darśibhiḥ, 'by the seers of the truth' — not Kṛṣṇa's private opinion, but what those who see reality as it is have always seen (dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ, 'the conclusion has been seen').

sentences.t:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति ॥
sentences.tr:
avināśi tu tat viddhi yena sarvam idam tatam |
vināśam avyayasya asya na kaścit kartum arhati ||

morph.gloss: that (tat: acc. sg. neut., referring to what pervades everything)
which (yena: instr. sg. neut. relative, 'by which')
to stretch, pervade (tatam: past participle, nom. sg. neut. 'pervaded')
imperishable, undecaying (avyayasya: gen. sg., referring to what pervades everything)
this (asya: gen. sg. neut.; avyayasya + a- → avyayasyā-)
to be able, deserve (arhati: present 3rd sg. 'is able to')

sentences.l: Indestructible, but, that know — by-which all this [world is] pervaded; the-destruction of-this imperishable-one no-one is-able to-bring-about.
sentences.i: But know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded; no one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable thing.
sentences.n: Tat, 'that', is the first naming — still unnamed as ātman — of the reality behind everything: whatever pervades (tatam, from the same root as the ordinary word for a thread or web) the whole visible world is what cannot be destroyed. Na kaścit kartum arhati, 'no one is able to bring it about', restates verse 16's dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ as a flat impossibility, just before the poem's most systematic listing of the self's indestructibility begins at verse 18. The same root tan returns in the metaphor of 7.7, where all things are said to be strung on Kṛṣṇa like jewels on a thread.

sentences.t:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः ।
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत ॥
sentences.tr:
antavantaḥ ime dehāḥ nityasya uktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ |
anāśinaḥ aprameyasya tasmāt yudhyasva bhārata ||

morph.gloss: having an end, finite, perishable (nom. pl. masc.; -aḥ before i- → elided, plain -a)
body (nom. pl. masc.; -āḥ before n- → -ā, visarga dropped)
eternal, permanent (nityasya: gen. sg., referring to the embodied self)
to speak, call (ukta: past participle 'said, called', nom. pl. masc.; -a + u- → -o-)
the embodied one, possessor of a body (gen. sg., in apposition to nityasya)
imperishable, undying (gen. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)

sentences.l: Having-an-end [are] these bodies, of-the-eternal called, of-the-embodied-one — of-the-imperishable, of-the-immeasurable; therefore fight, O Bhārata.
sentences.i: These bodies are said to have an end, but the embodied self that dwells in them is eternal, imperishable, immeasurable. Therefore fight, Bhārata.
sentences.n: The verse states the whole distinction the argument has been building toward: dehāḥ, 'bodies', are antavantaḥ, 'finite, ending'; the śarīrin/dehin who wears them is nitya, 'eternal', anāśin, 'undying', aprameya, 'immeasurable, beyond the reach of proof'. Tasmād yudhyasva, 'therefore fight', is the first time the command to fight is grounded explicitly in this metaphysics, rather than simply asserted as in verse 3.

sentences.t:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् ।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
yaḥ enam vetti hantāram yaḥ ca enam manyate hatam |
ubhau tau na vijānītaḥ na ayam hanti na hanyate ||

morph.gloss: who (yaḥ: nom. sg. masc. relative; -aḥ before e- → elided, plain -a)
this, him (enam: acc. sg. masc., referring to the self; used only in oblique cases)
who (yaḥ: nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + c- → -aś c-)
to kill (hata: past participle 'slain', acc. sg. masc.)
to know, understand (vijānītaḥ: present 3rd dual 'the two know'; -aḥ before n- → -o)
this, he (ayam: nom. sg. masc., referring to the self)
to kill (hanyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is killed')

sentences.l: Who him knows [as] the-slayer, and-who him thinks [to-be] slain — both-of-them do-not-understand: this-one does-not-kill, nor is-killed.
sentences.i: He who thinks this self a killer, and he who thinks it killed, both fail to understand: it does not kill, nor is it killed.
sentences.n: The famous couplet nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate, 'this [self] neither kills nor is killed', is quoted independently across Indian tradition; it answers, for the first time explicitly, the fear Arjuna raised in verse 4 (how can I kill Bhīṣma and Droṇa?) by denying that killing, in the relevant sense, ever touches the self at all — only the body. Hantāram, 'the slayer', and hatam, 'the slain', are exactly the two false views the verse rejects together.

sentences.t:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
sentences.tr:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit na ayam bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ |
ajaḥ nityaḥ śāśvataḥ ayam purāṇaḥ na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||

morph.gloss: to be born (jāyate: present middle 3rd sg.)
ever, at any time (-t + n- → -n n-)
to be, become (bhūtvā: gerund 'having come to be')
to be (bhavitā: periphrastic future 3rd sg. 'will come to be')
everlasting, perpetual (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
ancient, primeval (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
to kill (hanyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is killed')
to kill (hanyamāna: present passive participle, loc. sg. 'being killed')

sentences.l: It-is-not-born, nor does-it-die ever; nor, having-come-to-be, will-it ever-again cease-to-be — unborn, eternal, everlasting, this ancient one; it-is-not-killed when-the-body-is-being-killed.
sentences.i: It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come to be, it will never again cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
sentences.n: This verse states the self's unbornness and deathlessness as flatly as possible, in two parallel halves: na jāyate mriyate vā, then a run of four synonyms — ajaḥ, nityaḥ, śāśvataḥ, purāṇaḥ ('unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient') — for the same claim. The middle clause, na ayaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ, is the hardest to parse literally: 'nor, having come to be, will it cease to be again' — denying that the self even has the ordinary kind of existence that begins and could later end. This verse and the one before draw on a much older source: its second line is identical, word for word, to Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18, whose first line makes the same claim in different words (vipaścit for kadācit, kutaścin na babhūva kaścit for bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ).

sentences.t:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम् ।
कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम् ॥
sentences.tr:
veda avināśinam nityam yaḥ enam ajam avyayam |
katham saḥ puruṣaḥ pārtha kam ghātayati hanti kam ||

morph.gloss: to know (veda: perfect 3rd sg. used as present, 'knows'; veda + a- → vedā-)
who (yaḥ: nom. sg. masc. relative; -aḥ before e- → elided)
undecaying, imperishable, changeless (avyayam: acc. sg. masc.)
that, he (saḥ: nom. sg. masc.; the pronoun sa irregularly drops its visarga before any consonant)
to kill (ghātayati: causative present 3rd sg. 'causes to be killed, has killed')

sentences.l: Him-who-knows [as] indestructible, eternal, unborn, undecaying — who, that man, O Pārtha, how does-he-cause-to-be-killed whom, [or] kill whom?
sentences.i: How, Pārtha, can the man who knows this self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and undecaying, cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone himself?
sentences.n: The verse draws the practical conclusion from verses 19–20: if the self cannot be killed, a man who truly knows this (veda, a perfect used as a simple present, 'knows') cannot, in the relevant sense, be a killer at all — kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam, 'whom does he cause to be killed, [or] kill whom?', repeating kam for emphasis. Ghātayati, the causative of han, covers ordering or causing a killing as distinct from doing it directly; both are denied of the man of knowledge.

sentences.t:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि ।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
sentences.tr:
vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naraḥ aparāṇi |
tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇāni anyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī ||

morph.gloss: worn out, old, decayed (acc. pl. neut.)
to abandon, cast off (vihāya: gerund 'having cast off')
worn out, old (acc. pl. neut.; -i + a- → -y a-)
to go to, pass into (saṃyāti: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: As garments, worn-out, having-cast-off, new ones a-man takes, other [ones]; so bodies, worn-out, having-cast-off, other new [ones] passes-into, the-embodied-one.
sentences.i: Just as a man casts off worn-out garments and takes other, new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and passes into others that are new.
sentences.n: The chapter's most famous simile: the self changes bodies at death the way a person changes clothes — an image that returns the argument to the everyday after several verses of abstract metaphysics. Vāsāṃsi ('garments') and śarīrāṇi ('bodies') are matched term for term across the two half-lines, down to jīrṇāni ('worn out') and navāni ('new') repeated in both.

sentences.t:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः ।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः ॥
sentences.tr:
na enam chindanti śastrāṇi na enam dahati pāvakaḥ |
na ca enam kledayanti āpaḥ na śoṣayati mārutaḥ ||

morph.gloss: this, it (enam: acc. sg. masc., the self; the vulgate and BORI agree here — contrast the real variant at 2.26)
to become wet (kledayanti: causative present 3rd pl. 'they wet, moisten'; -i + ā- → -y ā-)
to dry up (śoṣayati: causative present 3rd sg. 'dries')

sentences.l: This-one weapons do-not-cut, this-one fire does-not-burn; and-this-one waters do-not-wet, [nor] wind dries-it.
sentences.i: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, nor does wind dry it.
sentences.n: The four elements each get their own verb and their own failure: chid ('cut') for weapons, dah ('burn') for fire, klid ('wet') for water, śuṣ ('dry') for wind — a rhetorical exhaustion of every physical way something could be destroyed, each denied of the self in turn.

sentences.t:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च ।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः ॥
sentences.tr:
acchedyaḥ ayam adāhyaḥ ayam akledyaḥ aśoṣyaḥ eva ca |
nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ sthāṇuḥ acalaḥ ayam sanātanaḥ ||

words.reading: acchedyaḥ ayam adāhyaḥ ayam akledyaḥ aśoṣyaḥ

glyphs.tr: acchedyaḥ ayam adāhyaḥ ayam akledyaḥ aśoṣyaḥ

morph.gloss: not to be cut, uncuttable (gerundive of chid with negative a-; nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
not to be burnt (gerundive of dah; nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
not to be wetted (gerundive of klid; nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
not to be dried (gerundive of śuṣ; nom. sg. masc.)
a fixed post, immovable, stationary (nom. sg. masc.; -uḥ + a- → -ur a-)
unmoving, immovable (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)

sentences.l: Uncuttable this, unburnable this, unwettable, undryable indeed and; eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving this, everlasting.
sentences.i: This self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried; it is eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving, everlasting.
sentences.n: The four negative gerundives (acchedya, adāhya, akledya, aśoṣya) restate verse 23's four elements as fixed attributes; five more epithets follow in the second line — the pile-up of near-synonyms (nitya, sanātana both 'eternal'; sthāṇu, acala both 'unmoving') is itself the rhetorical point: no single word is adequate, so the verse surrounds the self with as many as it can find.

sentences.t:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते ।
तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि ॥
sentences.tr:
avyaktaḥ ayam acintyaḥ ayam avikāryaḥ ayam ucyate |
tasmāt evam viditvā enam na anuśocitum arhasi ||

words.reading: avyaktaḥ ayam acintyaḥ ayam avikāryaḥ ayam ucyate

glyphs.tr: avyaktaḥ ayam acintyaḥ ayam avikāryaḥ ayam ucyate

morph.gloss: unmanifest (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
unthinkable, beyond thought (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
unchangeable, not subject to modification (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
to speak, call (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is called')
to deserve, ought (arhasi: present 2nd sg. 'you ought')

sentences.l: Unmanifest this, unthinkable this, unchangeable this, it-is-called; therefore, thus, having-known-it, not to-grieve-for-it you-ought.
sentences.i: This self is called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable. Knowing it to be so, you ought not to grieve.
sentences.n: Avyakta ('unmanifest'), acintya ('beyond thought') and avikārya ('unchangeable') push the description past the physical (verses 23–24) to declare the self beyond perception and even beyond conceptual grasp — a step that anticipates the language later used of brahman. The refrain nānuśocitum arhasi, 'you ought not to grieve', closes the argument opened at verse 11 and recurs, with small variations, through verse 30.

sentences.t:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम् ।
तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
sentences.tr:
atha ca enam nitya-jātam nityam vā manyase mṛtam |
tathā api tvam mahā-bāho na evam śocitum arhasi ||

morph.gloss: born (nitya-jāta: 'constantly born', acc. sg. masc., i.e. subject to endless rebirth)
to think (manyase: present middle 2nd sg. 'you think')
to die (mṛta: past participle 'dead', acc. sg. masc.)
thus, in this way (the vulgate reading; the BORI critical edition reads nainaṃ, na + enam 'this, it', in its place — see note)
to deserve, ought (arhasi: present 2nd sg. 'you ought')

sentences.l: But if, also, this-one [as] constantly-born or constantly dead you-think — even-so, you, O mighty-armed-one, thus you-ought-not to-grieve.
sentences.i: But even if you think of this self as constantly being born and constantly dying, even so, mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve like this.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa now argues from the opposite premise, as a fallback: even granting the ordinary view that the self is born and dies again and again (nitya-jātaṃ nityaṃ vā mṛtam — transmigration understood as brute recurring birth-and-death, rather than the deathless self of verses 19–25), grief is still unwarranted, because birth makes death certain and death makes rebirth certain, as the next verse goes on to say. The vulgate reads naivaṃ, 'not thus, not in this way', in the second line; the BORI critical edition reads nainaṃ (na + enam, 'should not grieve for it') in its place, which shifts what is denied from the manner of grieving to the self itself — a small but real difference in what the line says.

sentences.t:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च ।
तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
sentences.tr:
jātasya hi dhruvaḥ mṛtyuḥ dhruvam janma mṛtasya ca |
tasmāt aparihārye arthe na tvam śocitum arhasi ||

morph.gloss: to be born (jāta: past participle 'born', gen. sg. masc.)
certain, fixed, sure (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before m- → -o)
to die (mṛta: past participle 'dead', gen. sg. masc.)
unavoidable, not to be evaded (loc. sg.; -e + a- → -e with avagraha)

sentences.l: Of-the-born, indeed, certain [is] death; certain [is] birth of-the-dead, and; therefore, in-a-matter-unavoidable, not you ought to-grieve.
sentences.i: For the one who is born, death is certain; and for the one who dies, birth is certain. Therefore you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
sentences.n: A tightly reasoned couplet in the strict logical style the poem uses when closing an argument: birth entails death, death (on this view of recurring transmigration) entails birth, so the whole cycle is aparihārya, 'unavoidable' — as fixed as any law of nature, and no more fit an object for grief than winter following autumn.

sentences.t:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत ।
अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना ॥
sentences.tr:
avyakta-ādīni bhūtāni vyakta-madhyāni bhārata |
avyakta-nidhanāni eva tatra kā paridevanā ||

morph.gloss: beginning (avyakta-ādi: 'whose beginning is unmanifest', nom. pl. neut.; -a + ā- → -ā-)
middle (vyakta-madhya: 'whose middle is manifest', nom. pl. neut.)
end, death (avyakta-nidhana: 'whose end is unmanifest', nom. pl. neut.; -i + e- → -y e-)
to lament, wail (paridevanā: nom. sg. fem. 'lamentation')

sentences.l: Unmanifest-in-their-beginning [are] beings, manifest-in-their-middle, O Bhārata, unmanifest-in-their-end indeed; there what [room for] lamentation?
sentences.i: Beings are unmanifest before birth, manifest between birth and death, and unmanifest again after death, Bhārata. What is there in that to lament?
sentences.n: A third argument, from ordinary experience rather than metaphysics: whatever a being is before birth and after death is already unmanifest and unknown to us, and only the interval between (vyakta-madhya, 'manifest in the middle') is visible — so death returns a being to a state no stranger than the one it came from, and no more a cause for grief.

sentences.t:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेनमाश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः ।
आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः शृणोति श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित् ॥
sentences.tr:
āścaryavat paśyati kaścit enam āścaryavat vadati tathā eva ca anyaḥ |
āścaryavat ca enam anyaḥ śṛṇoti śrutvā api enam veda na ca eva kaścit ||

morph.gloss: wonder, marvel (āścaryavat: adverbial, 'as a wonder, wonderingly')
someone, a certain one (-t + e- → -d e-)
to speak of, tell of (vadati: present 3rd sg.)
to know (veda: perfect 3rd sg. used as present, 'knows')
anyone, someone (with na: 'no one at all')

sentences.l: As-a-wonder someone sees it, and-as-a-wonder someone-else speaks-of it, likewise; and-as-a-wonder another hears it; and-even having-heard, no-one at-all knows it.
sentences.i: One looks on this self as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet even having heard, no one truly knows it.
sentences.n: A verse built almost entirely from the one word āścaryavat, 'as a wonder, wonderingly', repeated for the seer, the speaker and the hearer alike; the final clause, śrutvāpy enaṃ veda na caiva kaścit, 'even having heard, no one at all knows it', admits, within the teaching itself, that the self it describes exceeds ordinary knowing — a note of humility rare in the chapter's otherwise confident argument.

sentences.t:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत ।
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
sentences.tr:
dehī nityam avadhyaḥ ayam dehe sarvasya bhārata |
tasmāt sarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvam śocitum arhasi ||

morph.gloss: not to be slain, inviolable (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)

sentences.l: The-embodied-one always inviolable this, in-the-body of-everyone, O Bhārata; therefore, for-all beings, not you ought to-grieve.
sentences.i: This embodied self, Bhārata, is always inviolable in everyone's body. Therefore you ought not to grieve for any being.
sentences.n: The section that began at verse 11 closes exactly where it started, restating nānuśocitum arhasi ('you ought not to grieve') one last time, now generalized from Bhīṣma and Droṇa to sarvāṇi bhūtāni, 'all beings' — the argument was never really only about this one battle. Verse 31 turns from what the self is to what Arjuna, as a kṣatriya, must do regardless.

sentences.t:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि ।
धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
svadharmam api ca avekṣya na vikampitum arhasi |
dharmyāt hi yuddhāt śreyaḥ anyat kṣatriyasya na vidyate ||

morph.gloss: to look at, consider (avekṣya: gerund 'having considered')
righteous, lawful, conforming to dharma (dharmyāt: abl. sg.; -t + h- → -d dh-)
battle, war (yuddhāt: abl. sg.; -t + ś- → -c ch-)
the better thing, good (nom. sg. neut.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
a member of the warrior class (gen. sg. 'for a kṣatriya')
to find, exist (vidyate: present passive 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: One's-own-dharma also, having-considered, not you-ought to-waver; for than-a-righteous battle, better other-thing for-a-kṣatriya not there-is-found.
sentences.i: And considering your own dharma too, you should not waver: for a kṣatriya, there is nothing better than a righteous war.
sentences.n: A second, entirely separate argument now begins, running to verse 38: not the metaphysics of the self, but Arjuna's sva-dharma, 'own dharma', kept untranslated per convention — the duty specific to his class and station. Dharmya, 'righteous, lawful', names this particular war as one fought for a just cause (to recover the Pāṇḍavas' kingdom), which is what makes the argument work: not every war would qualify.

sentences.t:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम् ।
सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yadṛcchayā ca upapannam svarga-dvāram apāvṛtam |
sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddham īdṛśam ||

morph.gloss: to come about, present itself (upapanna: past participle 'come, arrived', nom. sg. neut.)
door, gate (svarga-dvāra: 'the gate of heaven', nom. sg. neut.)
to open, throw open (apāvṛta: past participle 'opened', nom. sg. neut.)
a member of the warrior class (nom. pl.)
to obtain, get (labhante: present middle 3rd pl.)

sentences.l: By-chance and come, the-gate-of-heaven thrown-open; happy [are the] kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, [who] obtain a-battle such-as-this.
sentences.i: Happy are the kṣatriyas, Pārtha, who find, by sheer chance, a war like this — an open gate to heaven.
sentences.n: Yadṛcchayā copapannam, 'come about by mere chance', marks that this battle is not something Arjuna sought out — refusing it means throwing away, rather than merely declining, an opportunity that came unbidden. Svarga-dvāram apāvṛtam, 'the gate of heaven flung open', names the reward Vedic tradition offers a kṣatriya who dies fighting justly — a promise the poem will later, from verse 42 on, treat with some suspicion when it becomes the object of desire.

sentences.t:
अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि ।
ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥
sentences.tr:
atha cet tvam imam dharmyam saṃgrāmam na kariṣyasi |
tataḥ svadharmam kīrtim ca hitvā pāpam avāpsyasi ||

morph.gloss: to do (kariṣyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will do')
to abandon, give up (hitvā: gerund 'having abandoned')
to obtain, incur (avāpsyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will incur')

sentences.l: But if you this righteous battle will-not do, then, one's-own-dharma and fame, having-abandoned, sin you-will-incur.
sentences.i: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own dharma and your fame, you will incur sin.
sentences.n: The consequence side of the sva-dharma argument: refusing this particular fight is not neutral but an active abandonment (hitvā) of both dharma and kīrti, 'fame' — a warrior's two chief goods — incurring pāpa, 'sin, evil', in their place. The next three verses spell out exactly what form that lost fame and incurred sin will take among people who hear of Arjuna's refusal.

sentences.t:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम् ।
सम्भावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
akīrtim ca api bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te avyayām |
saṃbhāvitasya ca akīrtiḥ maraṇāt atiricyate ||

morph.gloss: to tell, narrate (kathayiṣyanti: future 3rd pl. 'they will tell of')
undying, unending, imperishable (avyayām: acc. sg. fem., agreeing with akīrtim; te + a- → te 'with avagraha)
to esteem, honor, respect (saṃbhāvita: causative past participle, gen. sg. 'of one who is honored')
to exceed, surpass (atiricyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is exceeded, surpasses')

sentences.l: Disgrace, and-also, [about-you] people will-tell, undying; and-of-one-honored disgrace than-death exceeds.
sentences.i: People will speak forever of your disgrace, and for a man once honored, disgrace is worse than death.
sentences.n: Akīrtim ... avyayām, 'disgrace ... undying', frames Arjuna's shame as a terrible immortality of its own, set against the true immortality of the self just taught in verses 12–30 — a bitter irony the verse leaves for the reader to notice. Saṃbhāvita, 'one held in high regard' (a causative past participle of bhū, 'to esteem'), is precisely Arjuna's own standing among his peers, which the argument says he is about to forfeit.

sentences.t:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः ।
येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम् ॥
sentences.tr:
bhayāt raṇāt uparatam maṃsyante tvām mahārathāḥ |
yeṣām ca tvam bahumataḥ bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam ||

morph.gloss: fear (bhayāt: abl. sg. 'out of fear'; -t + r- → -d r-)
battle (raṇāt: abl. sg. 'from battle'; -t + u- → -d u-)
to cease, withdraw (uparata: past participle, acc. sg. masc. 'withdrawn')
to think (maṃsyante: future middle 3rd pl. 'they will think')
highly esteemed, much thought of (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before bh- → -o)
to go (yāsyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will go')

sentences.l: Out-of-fear from-battle withdrawn they-will-think you, the-great-chariot-warriors; and-of-whom, you, highly-esteemed having-been, you-will-go [to] contempt.
sentences.i: The great warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and you will fall into contempt among those who once held you in high regard.
sentences.n: A social argument continues from verse 34: it is not fear itself but the appearance of fear, in the eyes of the very men Arjuna cares most about (mahārathāḥ, the great warriors of both armies), that the verse names as the real cost. Bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam, 'having been highly esteemed, you will go into contempt', measures the fall precisely by the height of Arjuna's present reputation.

sentences.t:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून्वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः ।
निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम् ॥
sentences.tr:
avācya-vādān ca bahūn vadiṣyanti tava ahitāḥ |
nindantaḥ tava sāmarthyam tataḥ duḥkhataram nu kim ||

morph.gloss: not to be said, unspeakable (first compound member)
word, remark (avācya-vāda: 'unspeakable words', acc. pl.; -n + c- → -ṃś c-)
to speak (vadiṣyanti: future 3rd pl. 'they will speak')
unfriendly, hostile; an enemy (nom. pl., literally 'not-well-wishing')
to revile, mock, blame (nindantaḥ: present participle, nom. pl. 'reviling'; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
more painful (comparative of duḥkha; nom. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: Unspeakable-words many they-will-speak, your ill-wishers, reviling your capability; than-that more-painful, then, what?
sentences.i: Your enemies will say many unspeakable things about you, mocking your ability; and what could be more painful than that?
sentences.n: Ahitāḥ, 'those without goodwill', is a euphemism for enemies proper; the verse imagines the Kauravas mocking Arjuna's sāmarthya, 'capability, prowess' — the one thing a kṣatriya's whole identity rests on. Duḥkhataraṃ nu kim, 'what could be more painful?', closes the social argument on its strongest note before the summary in verse 37.

sentences.t:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् ।
तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः ॥
sentences.tr:
hataḥ vā prāpsyasi svargam jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm |
tasmāt uttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛta-niścayaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to kill (hata: past participle 'slain', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before v- → -o)
to attain, gain (prāpsyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will attain')
to enjoy (bhokṣyase: future middle 2nd sg. 'you will enjoy')
to stand up, arise (uttiṣṭha: imperative 2nd sg. 'arise!')
resolve, determination, certainty (kṛta-niścaya: 'having made up one's mind', nom. sg. masc.)

sentences.l: Slain, or, you-will-attain heaven; or, having-conquered, you-will-enjoy the-earth; therefore arise, O son-of-Kuntī, for-battle with-resolve-made.
sentences.i: If killed, you will attain heaven; if victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore rise up, Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
sentences.n: The social argument closes on a claim that leaves Arjuna no losing option at all: slain, he wins heaven; victorious, he wins the earth. Kṛta-niścayaḥ, 'with his resolve made', anticipates the technical sense of niścaya (firm resolve) that the coming section on buddhi will build on.

sentences.t:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ ।
ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥
sentences.tr:
sukha-duḥkhe same kṛtvā lābha-alābhau jaya-ajayau |
tataḥ yuddhāya yujyasva na evam pāpam avāpsyasi ||

morph.gloss: loss, non-gain (lābha-alābha: acc. dual, 'gain and loss'; -a + a- → -ā-)
defeat, non-victory (jaya-ajaya: acc. dual, 'victory and defeat'; -a + a- → -ā-)
to join, engage, yoke (yujyasva: imperative middle 2nd sg. 'engage!')

sentences.l: Pleasure-and-pain equal having-made, gain-and-loss, victory-and-defeat, then for-battle engage; thus sin you-will-not-incur.
sentences.i: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, engage in battle; in this way you will not incur sin.
sentences.n: The first appearance of the equanimity this poem calls samatva ('the state of being equal, evenness'), applied here directly to the outcomes of battle: three pairs (sukha-duḥkhe, lābhālābhau, jayājayau) that together cover everything at stake. Verse 38 is a hinge: it still argues from the fruits of action, as verses 32–37 did, but its method — meeting every outcome with an equal mind — is exactly what verses 39–53 turn into a discipline in its own right, what later tradition calls niṣkāma karma, 'action without craving for its fruit', though that phrase itself is not the poem's own.

sentences.t:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु ।
बुद्ध्या युक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि ॥
sentences.tr:
eṣā te abhihitā sāṃkhye buddhiḥ yoge tu imām śṛṇu |
buddhyā yuktaḥ yayā pārtha karma-bandham prahāsyasi ||

morph.gloss: to state, declare (abhihitā: past participle, nom. sg. fem. 'declared'; te + a- → te 'with avagraha)

the analysis distinguishing self from body just taught, and the philosophical school built on it (loc. sg. 'with regard to Sāṃkhya'; kept as the proper name of this approach, alongside yoga in the same verse — see note)
understanding, discernment, the faculty of judgment (nom. sg.; -iḥ + y- → -ir y-)
yoga, discipline (loc. sg. 'with regard to yoga')
to yoke, join (yukta: past participle 'yoked, disciplined', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before y- → -o)
action, deed, ritual act (first compound member)
bondage, bond (karma-bandha: 'the bondage of action', acc. sg.)
to abandon, cast off, be rid of (prahāsyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will cast off')

sentences.l: This to-you has-been-declared in-Sāṃkhya, the-understanding; but this in-yoga hear — by-which understanding yoked, O Pārtha, the-bondage-of-action you-will-cast-off.
sentences.i: This is the understanding declared to you in Sāṃkhya; now hear it in yoga, disciplined by which you will cast off the bondage of action, Pārtha.
sentences.n: A hinge verse naming, for the first time, the two approaches the poem keeps returning to: Sāṃkhya, the analysis just given (verses 11–38, distinguishing self from body, duty from desire), and yoga, the discipline of acting that Kṛṣṇa now turns to teach — not two rival philosophies but two ways into the same understanding. Sāṃkhya is treated here as a proper name, alongside yoga, and left untranslated in both, per conventions.md's untranslated-term list, which now names sāṃkhya alongside dharma, yoga, brahman and the guṇas. Buddhi, 'discernment, judgment, resolve', becomes the chapter's central word from here to verse 53 and returns, transformed, in the description of the sthitaprajña beginning at verse 54.

sentences.t:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते ।
स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् ॥
sentences.tr:
na iha abhikrama-nāśaḥ asti pratyavāyaḥ na vidyate |
svalpam api asya dharmasya trāyate mahataḥ bhayāt ||

morph.gloss: loss, destruction (abhikrama-nāśa: 'loss of the effort begun', nom. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
to go backward, miscarry (pratyavāya: nom. sg. 'adverse result, harm'; -aḥ before n- → -o)
to find, exist (vidyate: present passive 3rd sg.)
very little, a mere trace (svalpam: nom. sg. neut., adverbial 'even a little')
to protect, save, rescue (trāyate: present middle 3rd sg.)
great (mahataḥ: abl. sg. neut.; -aḥ before bh- → -o)

sentences.l: Here of-undertaking-loss there-is-not; adverse-result not there-is-found; even-a-little of-this dharma protects from-great danger.
sentences.i: In this discipline no effort is ever lost, and no harm is ever done; even a little of this dharma protects one from great danger.
sentences.n: Iha, 'here', points back to the yoga just named in verse 39: unlike an ordinary ritual act, wasted (abhikrama-nāśa) if not completed correctly, an act done in this spirit has value even incomplete, since its value lies in the doing rather than in a specific external result.

sentences.t:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन ।
बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम् ॥
sentences.tr:
vyavasāya-ātmikā buddhiḥ ekā iha kuru-nandana |
bahu-śākhāḥ hi anantāḥ ca buddhayaḥ avyavasāyinām ||

morph.gloss: resolve, determination, firm decision (first compound member)
having the nature of, consisting of (fem. adjective; vyavasāya-ātmikā: 'of the nature of firm resolve', nom. sg. fem.; -a + ā- → -ā-)
understanding, discernment, resolve (nom. sg.; -iḥ + e- → -ir e-)
one, single (ekā: nom. sg. fem.; -ā + i- → -e-)
delight, joy (kuru-nandana: 'delight of the Kurus', addressed to Arjuna, vocative)
branch (bahu-śākhā: 'many-branched', nom. pl. fem.; -āḥ before h- → -ā, visarga dropped)
endless, infinite (anantāḥ: nom. pl. fem.; -āḥ + c- → -āś c-)
understanding, resolve (nom. pl.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
one without firm resolve, irresolute (gen. pl.)

sentences.l: Of-the-nature-of-firm-resolve, [is] the-understanding, single, here, O joy-of-the-Kurus; but many-branched and-endless [are] the-understandings of-those-without-firm-resolve.
sentences.i: In this discipline the resolve is single and firmly fixed, joy of the Kurus; but the thoughts of the irresolute branch out endlessly.
sentences.n: Ekā, 'single, one', against bahuśākhāḥ ... anantāḥ, 'many-branched and endless': the man of yoga has one settled buddhi (here closer to 'resolve' than 'intellect'), while the irresolute (avyavasāyinām) scatter their attention across countless competing aims — a contrast the next three verses illustrate with the ritualists who chase heaven through many rites rather than fixing on one thing.

sentences.t:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः ।
वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥
sentences.tr:
yām imām puṣpitām vācam pravadanti avipaścitaḥ |
veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha na anyat asti iti vādinaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to flower, blossom (puṣpita: past participle 'flowered, flowery', acc. sg. fem.)
to proclaim, utter (pravadanti: present 3rd pl.; -i + a- → -y a-)
doctrine, teaching, discourse (veda-vāda: 'the doctrine of the Veda', i.e. its ritual portion)
delighting in, devoted to (veda-vāda-rata: 'devoted to the ritual doctrine of the Veda', nom. pl.)
other (anyat: nom. sg. neut.; -t + a- → -d a-)
one who says, declares, maintains (nom. pl.)

sentences.l: This flowery speech which they-proclaim, the-undiscerning, devoted-to-the-doctrine-of-the-Veda, O Pārtha, [saying] 'there-is nothing-else', thus declaring —
sentences.i: The undiscerning, Pārtha, who delight in the flowery language of the Vedic ritualists and declare that there is nothing beyond it —
sentences.n: The sentence beginning here runs through verse 44, a long period typical of the poem's more argumentative stretches. Puṣpitāṃ vācam, 'flowery speech', is a pointed image: attractive, ornamented language that promises much while, the poem argues, missing the point. Veda-vāda-ratāḥ, 'devoted to the ritual doctrine of the Veda', targets not the Veda itself but a narrow, literalist reading of its ritual portion as though rites for heaven were the whole of it; Kṛṣṇa's own relation to the Veda is addressed again at verses 45–46.

sentences.t:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम् ।
क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति ॥
sentences.tr:
kāma-ātmānaḥ svarga-parāḥ janma-karma-phala-pradām |
kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulām bhoga-aiśvarya-gatim prati ||

morph.gloss: self, nature (kāma-ātman: 'whose nature is desire', nom. pl. masc.; -a + ā- → -ā-)
intent on, devoted to, having as one's highest aim (svarga-para: nom. pl. masc.; -āḥ before j- → -ā, visarga dropped)
giving, bestowing (janma-karma-phala-pradā: 'bestowing birth as the fruit of ritual action', acc. sg. fem., describing vācam)
abundant, full of (kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulā: 'full of various particular rites', acc. sg. fem.)
lordship, power, sovereignty (bhoga-aiśvarya: 'enjoyment and power'; -a + ai- → -ai-)
going, attainment, goal (bhoga-aiśvarya-gati: 'the attainment of enjoyment and power', acc. sg.)

sentences.l: Whose-nature-is-desire, having-heaven-as-their-highest-aim, [speech] giving-good-birth-as-the-fruit-of-action, full-of-various-particular-rites, toward the-attainment-of-enjoyment-and-power —
sentences.i: — men whose nature is desire, who look on heaven as their highest goal, who offer speech promising rebirth as the fruit of ritual action, and are full of specific rites aimed only at pleasure and power —
sentences.n: The sentence continues without its own finite verb, piling description onto the veda-vāda-ratāḥ of verse 42: kāma-ātmānaḥ, 'whose very self is desire', svarga-parāḥ, 'for whom heaven is the highest thing'. The critique is not of ritual as such but of ritual performed for these narrower ends (enjoyment, power, a better rebirth) rather than as an offering without expectation of return — the positive alternative verse 47 goes on to state.

sentences.t:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम् ।
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते ॥
sentences.tr:
bhoga-aiśvarya-prasaktānām tayā apahṛta-cetasām |
vyavasāya-ātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate ||

morph.gloss: attached, clinging (past participle of pra-sañj; bhoga-aiśvarya-prasakta: 'attached to enjoyment and power', gen. pl.)
that (tayā: instr. sg. fem., referring to the puṣpitā vāc of verse 42; -ā + a- → -ā-)
to carry away, steal (apahṛta: past participle 'carried away, stolen')
mind (apahṛta-cetas: 'whose mind is carried away', gen. pl.)
of the nature of (vyavasāya-ātmikā: nom. sg. fem.; -a + ā- → -ā-)
concentration, meditative absorption, a settled mind (loc. sg.)
to establish, arrange, ordain (vidhīyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is formed, established')

sentences.l: Of-those-attached-to-enjoyment-and-power, by-that [speech] whose-minds-are-carried-away — the-resolve-of-firm-nature in-concentration is-not established.
sentences.i: For men attached to enjoyment and power, their minds carried away by such talk, no firmly settled resolve is ever formed in concentration.
sentences.n: The long sentence from verse 42 finally reaches its main clause: for such men, no vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ ('single, firmly resolved understanding', the very thing praised in verse 41) can form in samādhi, 'a settled, concentrated mind' — the ritualists' scattered aims of verses 42–43 are the direct cause of the scattered buddhi verse 41 already criticized.

sentences.t:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन ।
निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान् ॥
sentences.tr:
traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ nistraiguṇyaḥ bhava arjuna |
nirdvandvaḥ nitya-sattva-sthaḥ nir-yoga-kṣemaḥ ātmavān ||

morph.gloss: the domain, condition or product of the three guṇas (first compound member; guṇa untranslated per convention)
domain, sphere, scope (traiguṇya-viṣaya: 'having the three guṇas as their domain', nom. pl. masc.; -āḥ before v- → -ā, visarga dropped)
the Veda(s), sacred scripture (nom. pl.; -āḥ before n- → -ā, visarga dropped)
free from the domain of the three guṇas (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before bh- → -o; guṇa untranslated per convention)
to be (bhava: imperative 2nd sg. 'be!'; bhava + a- → bhavā-)
a pair (of opposites); nir-dvandva 'free from the pairs of opposites' (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
purity, goodness, true being (one of the three guṇas, kept untranslated as guṇa-vocabulary)
standing, grounded in (nitya-sattva-stha: 'ever grounded in sattva', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
acquisition and preservation, security (yoga: 'getting'; kṣema: 'keeping safe'; nir-yoga-kṣema: 'without concern for gain and security', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before ā- → elided, plain -a)
possessed of self, self-possessed, master of oneself (nom. sg. masc.)

sentences.l: Having-the-three-guṇas-as-their-domain [are] the-Vedas; free-from-the-three-guṇas be, Arjuna — free-from-the-pairs-of-opposites, ever-grounded-in-sattva, without-concern-for-gain-and-keeping, self-possessed.
sentences.i: The Vedas deal with the domain of the three guṇas; be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna — free from the pairs of opposites, ever grounded in sattva, unconcerned with gain and security, master of yourself.
sentences.n: Guṇa (compounded here as trai-guṇya, 'the domain of the three guṇas') is left untranslated per convention, even though the poem does not name the three guṇas individually until chapter 14; here it means simply the whole domain of ordinary nature's conditions, of which sattva (also left untranslated as guṇa-vocabulary) is one. Nistraiguṇyaḥ, 'beyond the three guṇas', states more directly than before that the goal lies past the whole system Vedic ritual operates within, not merely past bad ritual. Yoga-kṣema, 'acquiring and keeping safe' — the getting and the guarding of possessions — has a long later life in Indian religious and economic vocabulary alike; freedom from concern for either marks the self-possessed (ātmavān) man.

sentences.t:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके ।
तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः ॥
sentences.tr:
yāvān arthaḥ udapāne sarvataḥ saṃpluta-udake |
tāvān sarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ ||

morph.gloss: as much as, however great (yāvān: nom. sg. masc.)
use, purpose, need (arthaḥ: nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before u- → elided, plain -a)
to flow together, overflow (saṃpluta: past participle 'flooded, overflowing')
water (saṃpluta-udaka: 'in a flood of water', loc. sg.; -a + u- → -o-)
just so much, that much (tāvān: nom. sg. masc.)
to know, understand (vijānat: present participle, gen. sg. 'who understands', agreeing with brāhmaṇasya)

sentences.l: As-much use [as there is] in-a-well, on-all-sides in-a-flood-of-water, so-much [use is there] in-all the-Vedas, for-a-brahmin who-understands.
sentences.i: As much use as there is in a well when water is flooding on every side, so much is the use of all the Vedas to a brahmin who understands.
sentences.n: A simile that qualifies, without rejecting, the Veda's value: once the whole country is under flood, a single well adds nothing — likewise, for the man who has reached the understanding just described, the Vedas add nothing beyond what he already has, though they were of real use to him before he arrived there. Vijānataḥ brāhmaṇasya, 'for a brahmin who understands', is the positive counterpart to the merely ritual brahmins criticized in verses 42–44.

sentences.t:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
sentences.tr:
karmaṇi eva adhikāraḥ te mā phaleṣu kadācana |
mā karma-phala-hetuḥ bhūḥ mā te saṅgaḥ astu akarmaṇi ||

morph.gloss: action, deed (karmaṇi: loc. sg. 'in action'; -i + e- → -y e-)
entitlement, right, authority, claim (adhikāraḥ: nom. sg.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
cause, motive (karma-phala-hetu: 'the motive of action's fruit', nom. sg.; -uḥ + bh- → -ur bh-)
to be (bhūḥ: aorist injunctive 2nd sg., with mā: 'do not be'; -ūḥ + m- → -ūr m-)
attachment, clinging (saṅgaḥ: nom. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
to be (astu: imperative 3rd sg. 'let there be'; -u + a- → -va-)

sentences.l: In action alone is your entitlement, never in its fruits; do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and let there be no attachment of yours to inaction.
sentences.i: Your claim is to the action itself, never to what comes of it. Do not act for the sake of results, and do not cling to not acting either.
sentences.n: The most quoted verse of the poem, and the summary of the teaching on action running through verses 38–53. Adhikāra, 'entitlement, the right or standing [to do something]', is a term from ritual law: one is qualified to perform a rite and claim its fruit, but Kṛṣṇa restricts the adhikāra itself to the doing, never the phala, 'fruit'. Mā karma-phala-hetur bhūḥ uses the aorist injunctive with mā (as already at verse 3, mā ... gamaḥ) for a sharp prohibition: 'never let the fruit of action be your motive'. The final clause guards against a possible misreading of everything just said — that if the fruit does not matter, one might as well stop acting — by forbidding attachment to akarman, 'inaction', just as firmly as attachment to the fruit; this concern is taken up at length in chapter 3.

sentences.t:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनंजय ।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgam tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya |
siddhi-asiddhyoḥ samaḥ bhūtvā samatvam yogaḥ ucyate ||

morph.gloss: standing, situated (yoga-stha: 'grounded in yoga', nom. sg. masc.)
failure, non-accomplishment (siddhi-asiddhi: loc. dual, 'in success and failure'; -i + a- → -y a-)
equal, even-minded, the same (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before bh- → -o)
yoga (nom. sg.; -aḥ before u- → elided, plain -a)
to speak, call (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is called')

sentences.l: Grounded-in-yoga, do actions, attachment having-abandoned, O Dhanaṃjaya; in-success-and-failure equal having-become — evenness [is what] yoga is-called.
sentences.i: Perform actions grounded in yoga, Dhanaṃjaya, having abandoned attachment, even-minded alike in success and failure — for evenness of mind is what is meant by yoga.
sentences.n: The chapter's one explicit definition of yoga (kept untranslated, as the technical term the poem is here naming): samatvaṃ yoga ucyate, 'evenness [of mind] is called yoga'. Siddhy-asiddhyoḥ, 'in success and failure', restates the three pairs of verse 38 as a single pair covering any outcome at all; yoga-sthaḥ, 'standing in yoga', frames the whole verse as instruction for how to act, not whether to.

sentences.t:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनंजय ।
बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः ॥
sentences.tr:
dūreṇa hi avaram karma buddhi-yogāt dhanaṃjaya |
buddhau śaraṇam anviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phala-hetavaḥ ||

morph.gloss: far, distant (dūreṇa: instr. sg., adverbial 'by far')
yoga (buddhi-yoga: 'the yoga of understanding', abl. sg.; -t + dh- → -d dh-)
to seek, look for (anviccha: imperative 2nd sg. 'seek!')
motive, cause (phala-hetu: 'motivated by the fruit', nom. pl.)

sentences.l: By-far, indeed, inferior [is] action than-the-yoga-of-understanding, O Dhanaṃjaya; in-understanding refuge seek — wretched [are those] motivated-by-the-fruit.
sentences.i: Action by itself is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, Dhanaṃjaya; seek refuge in understanding — pitiable are those who act for the fruit.
sentences.n: Buddhi-yoga, 'the yoga of understanding' (naming the whole discipline taught since verse 39), is here set explicitly above ordinary action performed with an eye to its fruit; kṛpaṇāḥ, 'wretched, pitiable' — the same root behind Arjuna's own kārpaṇya, 'weakness of spirit', at verse 7 — brands the fruit-seeker with the very word Arjuna used of his own collapse.

sentences.t:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते ।
तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम् ॥
sentences.tr:
buddhi-yuktaḥ jahāti iha ubhe sukṛta-duṣkṛte |
tasmāt yogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam ||

morph.gloss: yoked, endowed with (buddhi-yukta: 'joined to understanding', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before j- → -o)
to abandon, leave (jahāti: present 3rd sg.; -i + i- → -ī-)
well done, a good deed, merit (first compound member)
badly done, an evil deed, demerit (sukṛta-duṣkṛta: acc. dual, 'merit and demerit')
to join, engage (yujyasva: imperative middle 2nd sg. 'engage!')

sentences.l: Joined-to-understanding, one-abandons here [both] merit-and-demerit; therefore for-yoga engage — yoga [is] skill in-actions.
sentences.i: One who is joined to understanding leaves behind, in this very life, both merit and demerit. Therefore engage yourself in yoga — yoga is skill in action.
sentences.n: A second definition of yoga, as famous as verse 48's: yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam, 'yoga is skill in actions'. Sukṛta-duṣkṛte, 'merit and demerit', are the two kinds of result an ordinary ritual act accumulates; the buddhi-yukta, 'one joined to understanding', leaves both behind iha, 'right here, in this life', rather than only after death — the discipline pays off immediately, not merely in some future rebirth.

sentences.t:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः ।
जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम् ॥
sentences.tr:
karma-jam buddhi-yuktāḥ hi phalam tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ |
janma-bandha-vinirmuktāḥ padam gacchanti anāmayam ||

morph.gloss: born (karma-ja: 'born of action', acc. sg. neut.)
to be freed, released (vinirmukta: past participle, nom. pl. masc. 'freed')
to go (gacchanti: present 3rd pl.; -i + a- → -y a-)
free from disease, untroubled, sound (anāmayam: acc. sg. neut., agreeing with padam)

sentences.l: The-fruit-born-of-action, joined-to-understanding, indeed, having-abandoned, the-wise; freed-from-the-bondage-of-birth, to-the-place they-go untroubled.
sentences.i: The wise, joined to understanding, abandon the fruit born of action; freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the place beyond all trouble.
sentences.n: Padam ... anāmayam, 'the untroubled place', is one of the poem's early names for the goal itself, before it acquires more developed names later, such as brahman; janma-bandha, 'the bondage of birth [and rebirth]', is the condition the whole discipline is meant to release one from, stated here for the first time in so many words.

sentences.t:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति ।
तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च ॥
sentences.tr:
yadā te moha-kalilam buddhiḥ vyatitariṣyati |
tadā gantāsi nirvedam śrotavyasya śrutasya ca ||

morph.gloss: a thicket, dense tangle, confusion (moha-kalila: 'the tangle of delusion', acc. sg. neut.)
to cross over, cross beyond (vyatitariṣyati: future 3rd sg. 'will cross beyond')
to go, attain (gantāsi: periphrastic future 2nd sg. 'you will attain')
to hear (śrotavya: gerundive 'to be heard', gen. sg. neut.)
to hear (śruta: past participle 'heard', gen. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: When your the-tangle-of-delusion the-understanding will-cross-beyond, then you-will-attain indifference toward-what-is-to-be-heard and-what-has-been-heard.
sentences.i: When your understanding has crossed beyond the tangle of delusion, you will become indifferent to all that has been heard and all that is yet to be heard.
sentences.n: Śrotavyasya śrutasya ca, 'of what is to be heard and what has been heard', points at scriptural teaching generally, recalling the ritualists of verses 42–44; nirveda, 'disenchantment, indifference', names not apathy but the state of no longer needing to hear any more — the same relation to the Vedas already stated by the well-and-flood simile of verse 46.

sentences.t:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला ।
समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि ॥
sentences.tr:
śruti-vipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā |
samādhau acalā buddhiḥ tadā yogam avāpsyasi ||

morph.gloss: to be confused, go astray, be in conflict (vipratipanna: past participle 'confused, distracted', nom. sg. fem.)
concentration, meditative absorption (samādhau: loc. sg.; -au + a- → -āv a-)
to attain, obtain (avāpsyasi: future 2nd sg. 'you will attain')

sentences.l: Confused-by-scripture your, when it-will-stand unwavering; in-concentration unmoving, the-understanding, then yoga you-will-attain.
sentences.i: When your understanding, now confused by conflicting scripture, stands unwavering and unmoving in concentration, then you will attain yoga.
sentences.n: This closes the buddhi-yoga section begun at verse 39: the buddhi that was scattered by the many-branched claims of ritual scripture (śruti-vipratipannā, 'distracted by what is heard', echoing verses 41–44) finally becomes acalā, 'unmoving', in samādhi — the very state denied in verse 44 (buddhiḥ ... na vidhīyate) now affirmed. Yogam avāpsyasi, 'you will attain yoga', answers Arjuna's opening request (verse 7, 'tell me what is truly better') in the discipline's own terms, before the dialogue turns, at verse 54, to what such a man of settled understanding actually looks like.

sentences.t: अर्जुन उवाच
sentences.tr: arjuna uvāca
sentences.l: Arjuna said

morph.gloss: Arjuna, the third Pāṇḍava, the great archer (nom. sg.)

sentences.t:
स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव ।
स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम् ॥
sentences.tr:
sthita-prajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhi-sthasya keśava |
sthita-dhīḥ kim prabhāṣeta kim āsīta vrajet kim ||

morph.gloss: established, steady, fixed (past participle of sthā; first compound member)
wisdom, insight, discernment (sthita-prajña: 'one whose wisdom is steady', gen. sg. masc.)
speech, manner of speaking, description (nom. sg.)
standing, situated (samādhi-stha: 'situated in concentration', gen. sg. masc.)
thought, wisdom, mind (sthita-dhī: 'one of steady mind', nom. sg. masc.)
