to speak, converse (prabhāṣeta: optative middle 3rd sg. 'would he speak')
to sit, remain, abide (āsīta: optative middle 3rd sg. 'would he abide')
to go, walk (vrajet: optative 3rd sg. 'would he go')

sentences.l: Of-one-whose-wisdom-is-steady, what [is the] manner-of-speech, of-one-situated-in-concentration, O Keśava? [One] of-steady-mind, how would-he-speak, how would-he-abide, would-he-walk how?
sentences.i: What is the mark of a man whose wisdom is steady, who is settled in concentration, Keśava? How would such a man of steady mind speak, how would he sit, how would he walk?
sentences.n: After the long teaching on buddhi-yoga (verses 39–53), Arjuna asks a very practical question: what does such a man actually look like? Sthita-prajña, 'one whose wisdom stands firm', becomes the technical name (introduced here and defined at verse 55) for the portrait that fills the rest of the chapter. The three verbs — speak, sit, walk — ask about speech, stillness and motion in turn, and Kṛṣṇa's answer moves through all three.

sentences.t: श्रीभगवानुवाच
sentences.tr: śrībhagavān uvāca
sentences.l: The Blessed Lord said

morph.gloss: the Blessed One, the Lord — Kṛṣṇa's title as speaker (nom. sg. bhagavān; -n + u- written joined)

sentences.t:
प्रजहाति यदा कामान्सर्वान्पार्थ मनोगतान् ।
आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manaḥ-gatān |
ātmani eva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthita-prajñaḥ tadā ucyate ||

morph.gloss: to abandon completely, give up (prajahāti: present 3rd sg.)
mind (manaḥ: first compound member; -aḥ before g- → -o)
gone, entered (manaḥ-gata: 'that have entered the mind', acc. pl.)
self (ātmani: loc. sg. 'in the self'; -i + e- → -y e-)
to be satisfied (tuṣṭa: past participle 'satisfied, content', nom. sg. masc.)
wisdom (sthita-prajña: nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
to speak, call (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is called')

sentences.l: When he-abandons-completely all desires present-in-the-mind, O Pārtha, in-the-self alone by-the-self content — [he] one-whose-wisdom-is-steady then is-called.
sentences.i: When a man gives up completely all the desires that have entered his mind, Pārtha, content in the self alone by the self, he is then called one of steady wisdom.
sentences.n: The defining verse for sthita-prajña, answering Arjuna's question with a definition before the description proper begins: kāmān ... prajahāti, 'he abandons desires', and ātmani eva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ, 'content in the self alone by the self', without an external object — a self-sufficiency that returns in different words through verses 56–71.

sentences.t:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः ।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
duḥkheṣu anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ |
vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīḥ muniḥ ucyate ||

morph.gloss: sorrow, pain (duḥkheṣu: loc. pl.; -u + a- → -v a-)
not agitated, unperturbed (past participle of ud-vij with negative an-)
mind (anudvigna-manas: 'whose mind is unperturbed', nom. sg. masc.)
longing, craving, desire (vigata-spṛha: 'from whom craving has departed', nom. sg. masc.)
gone, departed, free from (past participle of vī, first compound member)
anger (vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodha: 'free from passion, fear and anger', nom. sg. masc.)
thought, mind (sthita-dhī: nom. sg. masc.; -iḥ + m- → -ir m-)
a sage, silent ascetic (nom. sg.; -iḥ + u- → -ir u-)
to speak, call (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is called')

sentences.l: Whose-mind-is-unperturbed in-sorrows, in-pleasures from-whom-craving-has-departed, free-from-passion-fear-and-anger — [he] the-steady-minded, a-sage, is-called.
sentences.i: One whose mind is not disturbed by sorrows and does not crave pleasures, who is free from passion, fear and anger — such a man is called a sage of steady mind.
sentences.n: The portrait continues with pairs answering how the sthita-prajña relates to duḥkha and sukha (echoing sama-duḥkha-sukham at verse 15): unmoved by suffering, uncraving of pleasure. Muni, 'a sage, a silent one' (from man, 'to think', but traditionally associated with silence), gives the sthitaprajña a second name, alongside dhīra (verses 13, 15), in this poem's family of words for the man of settled mind.

sentences.t:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम् ।
नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
sentences.tr:
yaḥ sarvatra anabhisnehaḥ tat tat prāpya śubha-aśubham |
na abhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

morph.gloss: without attachment, affectionless (anabhisnehaḥ: nom. sg. masc.; sarvatra + a- → sarvatrā-)
that (tat tat: acc. sg. neut. doubled, 'this or that', distributive; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
bad, inauspicious (śubha-aśubha: acc. sg. neut., 'good or bad'; -a + a- → -ā-)
to rejoice at, delight in (abhinandati: present 3rd sg.)
to stand firm, be established (pratiṣṭhita: past participle, nom. sg. fem. 'established, firmly set')

sentences.l: Who everywhere without-attachment, this-or-that having-obtained, good-or-bad, does-not-rejoice, does-not-hate — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
sentences.i: He who is everywhere without attachment, on meeting with anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hates — his wisdom is firmly established.
sentences.n: A general principle stated for the first time here: attachment (sneha) itself, not the specific quality of the outcome, is what has to go — the sthitaprajña meets good and bad alike, not because he cannot tell them apart but because he holds neither. Prajñā pratiṣṭhitā, 'wisdom firmly established', becomes a refrain closing several of the following verses (58, 61, 68), each time restating that the wisdom asked about at verse 54 rests on a different specific practice.

sentences.t:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
sentences.tr:
yadā saṃharate ca ayam kūrmaḥ aṅgāni iva sarvaśaḥ |
indriyāṇi indriya-arthebhyaḥ tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

morph.gloss: to draw together, withdraw (saṃharate: present middle 3rd sg.)
object (indriya-artha: 'sense-object', abl. pl. 'from sense-objects'; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
to stand firm, be established (pratiṣṭhita: past participle, nom. sg. fem.)

sentences.l: When he-draws-in, and this-one, [his] limbs, as-a-tortoise, wholly, the-senses from-the-objects-of-the-senses — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
sentences.i: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs from every side, he withdraws his senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly established.
sentences.n: The famous tortoise simile — kūrmo 'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ, 'like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side' — gives sense-withdrawal a single memorable image; the refrain prajñā pratiṣṭhitā closes the verse as it did verse 57.

sentences.t:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः ।
रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते ॥
sentences.tr:
viṣayāḥ vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ |
rasa-varjam rasaḥ api asya param dṛṣṭvā nivartate ||

morph.gloss: to turn away, withdraw, cease (vinivartante: present middle 3rd pl.)
abstaining from food; here, fasting from sense-objects (nirāhāra: gen. sg.)
excepting, leaving aside (rasa-varjam: adverbial acc., 'except the relish for them')
taste, relish, attraction (nom. sg.; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
supreme, highest (nom. sg. masc./neut., referring to the highest reality)
to turn back, cease (nivartate: present middle 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: The-sense-objects turn-away from-the-embodied-one who-abstains, except relish; even the-relish of-him, the-supreme having-seen, turns-back.
sentences.i: For one who abstains, the objects of the senses fall away, except the relish for them; but even that relish falls away once he has seen the supreme.
sentences.n: A qualification of verse 58's tortoise image: mere abstention (nirāhāra) removes the objects but can leave rasa, 'the relish, the taste for them', lingering underneath — full freedom comes only when even that relish drops away, and only on seeing param, 'the supreme'. This is the first hint in the sthitaprajña section that the discipline rests on a positive vision, not just self-control.

sentences.t:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः ।
इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः ॥
sentences.tr:
yatataḥ hi api kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ |
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabham manaḥ ||

morph.gloss: to strive, exert oneself (yatat: present participle, gen. sg. 'of one who strives'; -aḥ before h- → -o)
violent, turbulent, forcibly agitating (nom. pl. neut.)
to carry off, seize (haranti: present 3rd pl.)

sentences.l: Of-one-who-strives, indeed, even, O son-of-Kuntī, of-a-man discerning — the-senses, turbulent, carry-off forcibly the-mind.
sentences.i: For even the man of discernment who is striving hard, Kaunteya, the turbulent senses can forcibly carry off his mind.
sentences.n: A candid warning right after two verses that might sound reassuring: even the vipaścit, 'discerning man', who is actively yatataḥ, 'striving', is not safe — the indriyāṇi pramāthīni, 'turbulent senses', can overpower the mind by force (prasabham). This sets up the practical instruction of the next verse.

sentences.t:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः ।
वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
sentences.tr:
tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yuktaḥ āsīta mat-paraḥ |
vaśe hi yasya indriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

morph.gloss: that, them (tāni: acc. pl. neut., referring to indriyāṇi)
to restrain, control, curb (saṃyamya: gerund 'having restrained')
to yoke, discipline (yukta: past participle 'disciplined, controlled', nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before ā- → elided, plain -a)
to sit, remain, abide (āsīta: optative middle 3rd sg. 'should remain')
me (stem form of aham in compounds, first compound member)
highest, supreme (mat-para: 'having me as the highest aim', nom. sg. masc.)
who (yasya: gen. sg. masc. relative; -a + i- → -e-)
to stand firm, be established (pratiṣṭhita: past participle, nom. sg. fem.)

sentences.l: Them, all, having-restrained, disciplined he-should-remain, intent-on-me; for whose senses [are] in-control, his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
sentences.i: Having restrained them all, he should remain disciplined, intent on me; for the man whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
sentences.n: The instruction following directly from verse 60's warning: saṃyamya, 'having restrained', is the practical remedy for the senses' pull. Mat-paraḥ, 'intent on me [Kṛṣṇa]', is the poem's first direct call to fix one's attention on Kṛṣṇa personally, rather than only on the impersonal ātman or buddhi described so far — a note that becomes central only much later, from chapter 7 on.

sentences.t:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
sentences.tr:
dhyāyataḥ viṣayān puṃsaḥ saṅgaḥ teṣu upajāyate |
saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodhaḥ abhijāyate ||

morph.gloss: to meditate on, dwell upon (dhyāyat: present participle, gen. sg. 'of one dwelling upon'; -aḥ before v- → -o)
that, them (teṣu: loc. pl., referring to viṣayān; -u + u- → -ū-)
to arise, be born (upajāyate: present middle 3rd sg. 'arises')
to be born, arise (saṃjāyate: present middle 3rd sg.)
to arise, spring up (abhijāyate: present middle 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Of-one-dwelling-upon sense-objects, of-a-man, attachment to-them arises; from-attachment is-born desire, from-desire anger arises.
sentences.i: When a man dwells on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
sentences.n: The first links of a chain of causation running through this verse and the next — dhyāna (dwelling on an object) leads to saṅga (attachment), then kāma (desire), then krodha (anger) — each explicitly said to arise (jāyate, with various prefixes) from the one before, in the poem's clearest statement of exactly how a mind loses its footing.

sentences.t:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः ।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
sentences.tr:
krodhāt bhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohāt smṛti-vibhramaḥ |
smṛti-bhraṃśāt buddhi-nāśaḥ buddhi-nāśāt praṇaśyati ||

morph.gloss: to arise, come to be (bhavati: present 3rd sg.)
to become confused (saṃmoha: nom. sg. 'confusion, delusion')
wandering, confusion, loss (smṛti-vibhrama: 'loss of memory', nom. sg.)
falling away, lapse, loss (smṛti-bhraṃśa: 'lapse of memory', abl. sg.)
destruction, ruin (buddhi-nāśa: 'ruin of understanding', nom. sg.; -aḥ before b- → -o)
ruin, destruction (buddhi-nāśa: abl. sg. 'from the ruin of understanding')
to perish utterly (praṇaśyati: present 3rd sg. 'he perishes')

sentences.l: From-anger arises confusion, from-confusion loss-of-memory; from-loss-of-memory [comes] ruin-of-understanding, from-ruin-of-understanding he-perishes.
sentences.i: From anger comes confusion, from confusion the loss of memory; from loss of memory, the ruin of understanding, and from the ruin of understanding, a man is lost.
sentences.n: The chain from verse 62 completes itself: krodha, then saṃmoha, smṛti-vibhrama, buddhi-nāśa, and finally praṇaśyati, 'he perishes utterly' — each step named by the same jāyate/bhavati family of verbs, so that verses 62–63 read as a single mechanism rather than an abstract moral warning. Buddhi-nāśa, 'the ruin of understanding', is the exact opposite of the vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ prized since verse 41; the two verses trace, cause by cause, how one turns into the other.

sentences.t:
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन् ।
आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
rāga-dveṣa-viyuktaiḥ tu viṣayān indriyaiḥ caran |
ātma-vaśyaiḥ vidheya-ātmā prasādam adhigacchati ||

morph.gloss: separated from, free from (rāga-dveṣa-viyukta: 'freed from passion and aversion', instr. pl.; -aiḥ + t- → -ais t-)
to move, roam (caran: present participle, nom. sg. masc. 'moving among')
subject to control, governable (ātma-vaśya: 'brought under the self's control', instr. pl.; -aiḥ + v- → -air v-)
to be controlled, governable, disciplined (first compound member)
self (vidheya-ātman: 'one whose self is disciplined', nom. sg. masc.; -a + ā- → -ā-)
to attain, arrive at (adhigacchati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: But with-senses-freed-from-passion-and-aversion moving-among sense-objects, [his senses] brought-under-the-self's-control, one-whose-self-is-disciplined, attains tranquility.
sentences.i: But the disciplined man, moving among sense-objects with his senses freed from passion and aversion and under the control of his own self, attains tranquility.
sentences.n: Answering the danger of verses 60–63 without demanding total withdrawal from sense-objects (which verse 59 already showed to be insufficient by itself): the man who moves among objects rāga-dveṣa-viyuktaiḥ, 'with passion and aversion set aside', is safe precisely because it is the passion and aversion, not contact with the world itself, that starts the chain of ruin. Prasāda, 'clarity, tranquility' (also 'grace'), names the positive state that follows once that danger is removed, and becomes the pivot word of the next verse.

sentences.t:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते ।
प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते ॥
sentences.tr:
prasāde sarva-duḥkhānām hāniḥ asya upajāyate |
prasanna-cetasaḥ hi āśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate ||

morph.gloss: sorrow, pain (sarva-duḥkha: gen. pl., 'of all sorrows')
to abandon, cease (hāni: nom. sg. 'cessation, loss'; -iḥ + a- → -ir a-)
to arise (upajāyate: present middle 3rd sg.; -a + u- → -o-)
to become clear, tranquil (prasanna: past participle 'clear, tranquil', first compound member)
mind (prasanna-cetas: 'whose mind is clear', gen. sg.; -aḥ before h- → -o)
to become firmly settled, stand firm (paryavatiṣṭhate: present middle 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: In-tranquility, of-all-sorrows the-cessation, of-him, arises; for of-one-of-tranquil-mind, quickly, the-understanding becomes-firmly-settled.
sentences.i: In that tranquility, all his sorrows come to an end; for the understanding of a man whose mind is tranquil quickly becomes firmly settled.
sentences.n: Prasāda, the tranquility attained at the end of verse 64, is now shown to cause two further goods: the end of all sorrow, and a buddhi that settles quickly (āśu) — a positive chain of causation answering the negative one of verses 62–63 point for point.

sentences.t:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना ।
न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम् ॥
sentences.tr:
na asti buddhiḥ ayuktasya na ca ayuktasya bhāvanā |
na ca abhāvayataḥ śāntiḥ aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham ||

morph.gloss: contemplation, meditative power, imaginative faculty (nom. sg.)
one without meditative power, uncontemplative (present participle of bhū causative with negative a-; gen. sg.)

sentences.l: There-is-not understanding for-the-undisciplined, and-not for-the-undisciplined [is there] contemplative-power; and-for-one-without-contemplative-power [there is] no peace; for-one-without-peace, whence [could there be] happiness?
sentences.i: The undisciplined man has no understanding, and no power of contemplation either; without contemplation there is no peace, and without peace, how can there be happiness?
sentences.n: A chain of negatives mirroring, in reverse, the positive chain of verses 64–65: the undisciplined (ayukta) lack buddhi and bhāvanā; without bhāvanā there is no śānti; without śānti no sukha. This closes the sthitaprajña section's argument proper before the final image of the ocean in verse 70.

sentences.t:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनु विधीयते ।
तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि ॥
sentences.tr:
indriyāṇām hi caratām yat manaḥ anu vidhīyate |
tat asya harati prajñām vāyuḥ nāvam iva ambhasi ||

morph.gloss: to move, roam (carat: present participle, gen. pl. 'roaming')
which (yat: nom. sg. neut. relative; -t + m- → -n m-)
to direct, ordain; here 'to be carried along, follow' (vidhīyate: present passive 3rd sg.)
that (tat: nom. sg. neut., referring to manaḥ; -t + a- → -d a-)
to carry off, seize (harati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Of-the-senses, indeed, roaming, which mind follows — that carries-off his wisdom, as-wind a-boat on-the-water.
sentences.i: When the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries off a man's wisdom, as the wind carries off a boat on the water.
sentences.n: A second memorable image, after the tortoise of verse 58: vāyur nāvam ivāmbhasi, 'like wind carrying off a boat on the water' — the mind that trails after the roving senses is as helpless as an unmanned boat in a gale. This restates, in one simile, the whole mechanism of verses 60–63.

sentences.t:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
sentences.tr:
tasmāt yasya mahā-bāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ |
indriyāṇi indriya-arthebhyaḥ tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

morph.gloss: to restrain, hold back (nigṛhīta: past participle 'restrained', nom. pl. neut.)
to stand firm, be established (pratiṣṭhita: past participle, nom. sg. fem.)

sentences.l: Therefore, of-whom, O mighty-armed-one, restrained wholly [are] the-senses from-the-objects-of-the-senses — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
sentences.i: Therefore, mighty-armed one, the man whose senses are wholly restrained from their objects — his wisdom is firmly established.
sentences.n: A closing restatement of verse 58's tortoise principle in plain terms, without the simile, as the sthitaprajña portrait turns toward its final image (the ocean of verse 70) and conclusion (verses 71–72). Mahābāho, 'mighty-armed one', addressed to Arjuna the warrior, quietly reminds the listener that this teaching on inward restraint is meant for a man about to fight, not a renunciant withdrawing from the world.

sentences.t:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी ।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥
sentences.tr:
yā niśā sarva-bhūtānām tasyām jāgarti saṃyamī |
yasyām jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyataḥ muneḥ ||

morph.gloss: being, creature (sarva-bhūta: gen. pl., 'of all beings')
to be awake, watch (jāgarti: present 3rd sg.)
to see (paśyat: present participle, gen. sg. 'of the one who sees'; -aḥ before m- → -o)

sentences.l: What [is] night for-all-beings, in-that the-self-controlled-one is-awake; in-which beings are-awake, that [is] night for-the-seeing sage.
sentences.i: What is night for all beings, in that the disciplined man is awake; and what all beings are awake to, that is night for the sage who sees.
sentences.n: A verse built entirely on a paradoxical reversal of niśā, 'night', and jāgṛ, 'to be awake' — the sthitaprajña is awake to a reality that ordinary beings sleep through, and asleep (uninterested) in the ordinary pursuits that keep them awake. Muni, 'sage', returns from verse 56 to close the portrait's central section with the same word it began with.

sentences.t:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् ।
तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी ॥
sentences.tr:
āpūryamāṇam acala-pratiṣṭham samudram āpaḥ praviśanti yadvat |
tadvat kāmāḥ yam praviśanti sarve saḥ śāntim āpnoti na kāma-kāmī ||

morph.gloss: to fill up (āpūryamāṇa: present passive participle 'being filled', acc. sg. neut.)
foundation, base (acala-pratiṣṭha: 'whose base is unmoving', acc. sg. neut.)

sentences.l: Being-filled, whose-foundation-is-unmoving, the-ocean, waters enter, just-as; likewise desires whom enter, all — he attains peace, not the-desirer-of-desires.
sentences.i: As waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet stays unmoving in its depths, so all desires enter the man who attains peace — not the man who desires desires.
sentences.n: The chapter's second great simile for the sthitaprajña, after the tortoise of verse 58: the ocean, into which every river empties without ever overflowing or being disturbed (acala-pratiṣṭham, 'unmoving in its foundation'), receives desires the way it receives rivers — without being moved by them. Kāma-kāmī, 'a desirer of desires' (one who chases wanting itself), is set against the man who has attained śānti; both closing words look back to kāma at the start of the chain in verse 62.

sentences.t:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान् पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः ।
निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
vihāya kāmān yaḥ sarvān pumān carati niḥspṛhaḥ |
nirmamaḥ nirahaṃkāraḥ saḥ śāntim adhigacchati ||

to move, live, act (carati: present 3rd sg.)

free from the sense of 'mine', unpossessive (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before n- → -o)

sentences.l: Having-abandoned desires, who all, a-man lives free-from-longing; without-mine-ness, without-egoism, he attains peace.
sentences.i: The man who abandons all desires and lives free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' or of 'I' — he attains peace.
sentences.n: Nirmamaḥ, 'without mine-ness', and nirahaṃkāraḥ, 'without egoism' (literally 'the I-maker'), name the two possessive structures — ownership and selfhood — that the discipline since verse 55 has been dismantling; the verse effectively restates verse 55's definition (ātmani eva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ) with the emphasis now on what has been let go rather than on what remains.

sentences.t:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति ।
स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha na enām prāpya vimuhyati |
sthitvā asyām anta-kāle api brahma-nirvāṇam ṛcchati ||

morph.gloss: pertaining to brahman, divine, brahmic (fem. adjective; brahman kept untranslated per convention)
this, it (enām: acc. sg. fem., referring to sthitim; BORI reads the same nainām here, unlike the real variant at 2.26)
to be deluded, confused (vimuhyati: present 3rd sg.)
this (asyām: loc. sg. fem., referring to sthitim)

brahman, the absolute (first compound member; kept untranslated per convention)
extinguishing, blowing out (of a flame), beatitude (brahma-nirvāṇa: 'the beatitude of brahman', acc. sg.)

sentences.l: This [is] the-brahman-state, O Pārtha; not-it having-attained, one-is-deluded. Having-remained in-this even at-the-time-of-death, the-beatitude-of-brahman one-reaches.
sentences.i: This is the state that is brahman, Pārtha; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Remaining in it even at the hour of death, one reaches the beatitude of brahman.
sentences.n: The chapter's closing verse names the sthitaprajña's condition brāhmī sthitiḥ, 'the brahman-state' — the first appearance of brahman (kept untranslated per convention) in the poem, quietly identifying the steady wisdom described since verse 55 with the highest reality itself, not treating it as merely a psychological achievement. Brahma-nirvāṇam, 'the nirvāṇa that is brahman' (nirvāṇa literally 'blown out', as a flame is extinguished), uses a word later strongly associated with Buddhism in a purely Vedāntic sense here; anta-kāle 'pi, 'even at the moment of death', promises that this state, reached even once at the very end, is enough — closing the chapter's whole argument, which began with Arjuna's fear of death, by placing death itself inside a state that fear can no longer touch.

glossary.शान्तिमाप्नोति: śāntim āpnoti — śānti — peace, calm (acc. sg.); āp — to obtain, attain (āpnoti: present 3rd sg.)
glossary.कामकामी: kāma-kāmī — kāma — desire (first compound member); kāmin — desiring, one who desires (kāma-kāmin: 'one who desires desires', nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.कामान्यः: kāmān yaḥ — kāma — desire (kāmān: acc. pl.); yad — who (yaḥ: nom. sg. masc. relative)
glossary.पुमांश्चरति: pumān carati — puṃs — a man (pumān: nom. sg.; -n + c- → -ṃś c-); car — to move, live, act (carati: present 3rd sg.)
glossary.निःस्पृहः: niḥspṛhaḥ — niḥ-spṛha — free from longing, without craving (nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.निर्ममो: nirmamaḥ — nir-mama — free from the sense of 'mine', unpossessive (nom. sg. masc.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
glossary.निरहंकारः: nirahaṃkāraḥ — nir-ahaṃkāra — free from egoism, without self-assertion (nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.शान्तिमधिगच्छति: śāntim adhigacchati — śānti — peace, calm (acc. sg.); adhi-gam — to attain, arrive at (adhigacchati: present 3rd sg.)
glossary.ब्राह्मी: brāhmī — brāhmī — pertaining to brahman, divine, brahmic (fem. adjective; brahman kept untranslated per convention)
glossary.स्थितिः: sthitiḥ — sthiti — state, condition, standing firm (nom. sg.)
glossary.नैनां: na enām — na — not (na + e- → nai-); enad — this, it (enām: acc. sg. fem., referring to sthitim; BORI reads the same nainām here, unlike the real variant at 2.26)
glossary.प्राप्य: prāpya — pra-āp — to attain, reach (prāpya: gerund 'having attained')
glossary.विमुह्यति: vimuhyati — vi-muh — to be deluded, confused (vimuhyati: present 3rd sg.)
glossary.स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि: sthitvā asyām anta-kāle api — sthā — to stand, remain (sthitvā: gerund 'having remained'); idam — this (asyām: loc. sg. fem., referring to sthitim); anta — end (first compound member); kāla — time (anta-kāla: 'the time of the end', loc. sg. 'at death'); api — even (kāle + a- → kāle 'with avagraha)
glossary.ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति: brahma-nirvāṇam ṛcchati — brahman — brahman, the absolute (first compound member; kept untranslated per convention); nirvāṇa — extinguishing, blowing out (of a flame), beatitude (brahma-nirvāṇa: 'the beatitude of brahman', acc. sg.); ṛ — to reach, attain (ṛcchati: present 3rd sg.)

about: Sāṅkhyayoga, "the yoga of knowledge," is the Gītā's philosophical hinge: Arjuna has laid down his bow, and Kṛṣṇa spends the whole chapter answering his despair before a single arrow is fired. The teaching moves in three movements. First Kṛṣṇa argues that the self (ātman) that inhabits the body is unborn and undying, untouched by the weapons that can only reach the body it wears, so that grief for the dead or fear of killing rests on a mistake about what a person really is (verses 11–30). He then turns to Arjuna's standing as a kṣatriya, arguing that a warrior has nothing better than a battle fought in a just cause, and that refusing it brings both sin and lasting disgrace (verses 31–38). From there the chapter opens its second and more lasting teaching: action performed without attachment to its fruit, buddhi-yoga, "the yoga of understanding," culminating in the single most quoted verse of the poem, on the right to the act itself but never to its results (verse 47). The chapter closes with a portrait of the sthitaprajña, "the man of steady wisdom," whose senses are drawn in like a tortoise's limbs and whose mind receives the world's desires the way the ocean receives rivers, without being disturbed — ending on the promise that this settled state is itself a share in brahman, reachable even at the hour of death.
